title: Dynamic Graph Neural Networks for Autonomous Robot Navigation
abstract: Autonomous robot navigation necessitates robust perception and decision-making capabilities that can adapt to dynamic and unpredictable environments. Traditional graph neural networks (GNNs) often rely on static graph structures, failing to effectively represent and reason about the constantly evolving relationships within a robot's surroundings. This paper proposes a novel framework utilizing Dynamic Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) to address this limitation. The DGNN architecture incorporates dynamically adjusted node and edge attributes, driven by sensor data and the robot's internal state. This allows for real-time adaptation of the graph representation, improving the robot's ability to accurately perceive its environment and make informed navigation decisions. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical analysis and a detailed specification of the DGNN design, emphasizing its advantages over static GNNs. The core claim is that static GNNs cannot adapt to the constantly changing environment experienced by autonomous robots. The key mechanism is the utilization of a GNN architecture with dynamically adjusted node and edge attributes based on sensor data and the robot's internal state, allowing for real-time adaptation of the graph representation.

title: Nonlinear Geometry and Quantum Computing: A Connection
abstract: This paper explores the synergistic relationship between nonlinear geometry and quantum computing, focusing on the potential of utilizing topological structures to enhance quantum computation's capabilities and efficiency. We introduce a novel approach centered around the application of topological optimization algorithms to manipulate qubit arrangements, aiming to improve both precision and operational efficiency. The core mechanism involves the strategic implementation of topological constraints within the qubit configuration, leveraging the inherent robustness of these structures to mitigate errors and improve overall computation performance. The research addresses the limitations of current quantum algorithms by proposing a fundamentally different approach, promising significant advancements in the scalability and effectiveness of quantum information processing. This work details the design of a quantum algorithm based on self-spinning quantum states, demonstrating a viable pathway toward extended quantum computation through the integration of topological principles.

title: Decentralized Federated Learning with Byzantine Fault Tolerance via Differential Privacy
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data sources without directly sharing the data itself. However, existing FL systems face significant vulnerabilities, including malicious participant attacks and data breaches. This paper proposes a novel decentralized federated learning framework that integrates Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) protocols, inspired by blockchain technology, with differential privacy (DP) mechanisms. The core claim is that this synergistic combination provides a substantially more robust and secure FL paradigm. Specifically, the system utilizes BFT to detect and mitigate malicious behavior from participants, ensuring data integrity and model robustness, while DP safeguards user privacy by adding controlled noise to the model updates. This framework allows the system to tolerate a certain number of Byzantine failures while maintaining accurate models. The system architecture is decentralized, eliminating a single point of failure and enhancing overall resilience. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline a conceptual implementation strategy.

title: Layer-Wise Gate-Controlled Prompt Truncation in a Multimodal Chest X-Ray Classifier
abstract: Mixture of Prompt Experts (MoPE) adapts multimodal transformers through input-dependent prompt composition, while retaining a fixed prompt length. We investigate a layer-wise gating extension in a binary chest X-ray classification pilot study. The controller predicts a retention ratio for each sample, averages these ratios within a mini-batch, and uses the resulting integer length to truncate the static and mixed visual prompts. Retained mixed prompts are also scaled by the individual ratios. In one recorded run per configuration, the gated model reached a best validation accuracy of 0.8996, compared with 0.8969 for the fixed-length baseline; the corresponding final values were 0.8963 and 0.8802. The exported gate statistics imply a retained length of one at all recorded training points, relative to a configured maximum of six. This reduces the complete visual sequence from 210 to 200 tokens, but no direct runtime measurements establish an acceleration benefit. Report-derived labels, report text as input, sequential data partitioning, and the absence of repeated controlled experiments limit interpretation. The findings document prompt shortening under the configured gate penalty; they do not establish sample-specific length allocation, superiority over fixed short prompts, or clinical utility. Code is available at: https://github.com/jingtaolei/mope-dynamic-prompt-truncation.

title: FrankenReport: Early Exiting in Long-Form Generation Using Expected Value of Computation
abstract: While deep research systems address interactive information-seeking needs impressively, their real-world deployments face latency and resource-consumption challenges. We present FrankenReport, an interface for long-form knowledge-seeking report generation that supports adaptive early exiting per section: it evaluates intermediate outputs during generation and predicts whether further targeted computation will yield significant quality gains. In a simulation study, FrankenReport outperforms random allocation baselines by a large margin (up to 4x) under low budgets and smoothly recovers full-pipeline quality as the budget grows, showing that future quality gains are predictable from intermediate drafts. Through experiments and user studies, we further show that despite varying preferences across users and topics, FrankenReport adapts to simple, natural user feedback as efficiently as methods requiring much costlier supervision such as generated drafts and explicit rationales.

title: What Matters in Orchestrating Robot Policies: A Systematic Study of Hierarchical VLA Agents
abstract: Hierarchical vision-language-action (Hi-VLA) systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for complex robot manipulation, by using high-level VLM planners to decompose tasks into language subgoals executed by low-level VLA controllers. Despite recent empirical progress, there is a lack of unified design principles for these systems: existing Hi-VLA systems differ in how they choose and connect planners, controllers, mechanisms to switch between the two, and how observations and memory are represented in the planner. In this paper, we present a systematic study of Hi-VLA design for robot manipulation. We unify representative Hi-VLA agents under an options-style control framework and benchmark core design choices across short-horizon, long-horizon, and reasoning-intensive tasks. Our analysis distills practical principles for building Hi-VLA systems, showing how model choices and interface mechanisms jointly shape performance. Applying these principles yields a substantially stronger system than either flat VLA control or a naively designed hierarchy, across experiments both in simulation and on a real ALOHA robot. Overall, our results provide a foundation for building more capable, robust, and principled hierarchical VLA agents. More information and video at jiahenghu.github.io/hi-vla.

title: Quantum Entanglement Geometry Quantization
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents a profound challenge to our understanding of information and computation. This research investigates the geometric properties of quantum entanglement, proposing a novel model – Quantum Entanglement Geometry Quantization (QGC) – that leverages entanglement to predict and optimize quantum computation processes. We explore the potential of QGC to provide a more efficient and robust framework for information transfer and processing, offering a significant advancement over traditional approaches. The core mechanism centers around constructing a geometric representation of entangled states, predicting key properties of quantum entanglement, and ultimately, suggesting potential applications within quantum algorithms and quantum information theory. This paper presents a preliminary analysis, demonstrating the potential of QGC to offer a new perspective on entanglement's impact on computation.

title: Title: Universal Quantum State Transformation via Wave Function Synthesis
abstract: Quantum state transformation is a fundamental process in quantum mechanics, crucial for manipulating and analyzing quantum states. Traditional methods often rely on predefined transformations, limiting their applicability to specific scenarios. This paper proposes a novel approach to quantum state transformation – Wave Function Synthesis (WFS) – which utilizes a dynamic generation of transformation maps to enable the mapping of quantum states to each other. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of theoretical and experimental analyses, highlighting its potential for creating a universal mapping system. WFS offers a more flexible and powerful approach compared to existing transformation techniques, addressing limitations in current state representation and manipulation.

title: Quantum Entanglement Phase Correction: An Adaptive Approach to Error Mitigation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, offers the potential for unparalleled computational power. However, its delicate nature necessitates careful management of quantum states to minimize errors. This paper introduces a novel quantum error correction algorithm, Quantum Entanglement Phase Correction (QEP), predicated on the inherent adaptability of quantum entanglement. We propose a method that leverages the self-adjusting nature of entangled states to actively correct errors during quantum information processing. This approach significantly reduces the impact of decoherence and other sources of error, ultimately enhancing the precision and robustness of quantum computations. The proposed QEP algorithm offers a promising pathway toward more reliable and accurate quantum information handling, addressing a critical challenge in the field of quantum technology.

title: Core Claim: Researching non-linear topological quantum computation using adaptive geometric simplification techniques, automatically adjusting topological structure during computation to reduce computational complexity and improve efficiency.
abstract: The development of quantum computing has spurred significant research into novel computational paradigms, particularly those leveraging topological quantum systems. Non-linear topological quantum computation offers a promising pathway to enhanced computational power due to its inherent robustness against local noise. This paper investigates a novel approach to improve the efficiency of non-linear topological quantum computation by employing adaptive geometric simplification. We propose a sophisticated algorithm that dynamically adjusts the topology of the underlying quantum system during the computation process, minimizing the number of required steps and ultimately enhancing computational performance. This work addresses a critical challenge in the field – the inherent computational complexity associated with traditional topological quantum algorithms – through the introduction of self-adjusting geometric simplification. We analyze the benefits of this approach in a specific model, demonstrating a significant reduction in computational cost compared to existing methods. The research explores the interplay between topological properties, geometric simplification, and the efficiency of quantum computations. The focus is on developing a practical and scalable algorithm that can be applied to a broader range of non-linear topological quantum systems. The core mechanism involves a self-optimizing geometric simplification algorithm that adjusts the system's topology in real-time, thereby reducing computational bottlenecks.

The paper details the algorithm's core mechanisms, provides a theoretical foundation for its efficacy, and presents a comprehensive evaluation of its performance on various datasets. The core claim is that CAML significantly surpasses existing methods in terms of prediction accuracy and robustness, offering a more sophisticated and adaptable approach to machine learning.

title: Title: Temporal Recurrence Network (TRN) for Data Compression
abstract: This paper presents the Temporal Recurrence Network (TRN), a novel data compression technique that leverages dynamic network adjustments based on temporal patterns within datasets. Traditional compression algorithms often rely on static compression methods, failing to effectively exploit the inherent sequential structure of data. The TRN employs a neural network trained to predict future data changes, creating a 'temporal graph' that compresses data by leveraging these learned predictions. This approach offers enhanced compression efficiency and robustness compared to existing methods, particularly when dealing with data exhibiting significant temporal dependencies. The paper details the architecture, training process, and experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of the TRN in various data compression scenarios.

title: Quantum Decoherence Modeling Based on Probabilistic Models
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to modeling quantum decoherence using probabilistic models. Traditional quantum decoherence models often rely on simplified assumptions, leading to inaccuracies in predicting decoherence times. This work introduces a more rigorous framework based on statistical physics principles, explicitly incorporating probabilistic elements to capture the complex dynamics of quantum systems. The core of the model lies in formulating decoherence as a probabilistic process, allowing for a more accurate quantification of the rate at which quantum information is lost. We derive key equations that describe the evolution of the quantum state under the influence of various decoherence mechanisms. The model's parameters are determined through statistical analysis of the underlying quantum system, providing a predictive capability for decoherence times. Simulation results demonstrate the improved accuracy of this probabilistic approach compared to conventional models. This work represents a significant advancement in quantum decoherence modeling, offering a more reliable tool for designing and analyzing quantum computing architectures and quantum information processing protocols.

title: Symmetry Geometry Transformations and Multi-Body Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper investigates the application of symmetry geometry transformations within the context of multi-body quantum entanglement. The core claim is that these transformations can mitigate the detrimental effects of entanglement degradation, offering a novel approach to quantum information transfer and processing. We explore the potential of employing these transformations to reduce the vulnerability of entangled states, ultimately enhancing the fidelity and stability of quantum systems. The study focuses on demonstrating the efficacy of a specific transformation – a geometric shift – in reducing entanglement entropy and preserving quantum information. The research aims to contribute to the theoretical understanding of entanglement protection and provides a potential pathway for improved quantum technologies.

title: Title: Adaptive Natural Language Processing for Text Sentiment Analysis
abstract: This research investigates the application of an adaptive natural language processing (NLP) framework for text sentiment analysis. Traditional sentiment analysis methods often struggle with the inherent complexity and nuances of human language, requiring extensive feature engineering and model training. This paper proposes a dynamic adaptive NLP framework that dynamically adjusts model parameters and features based on the characteristics of the input text data. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously optimizes the model's performance through an iterative process of data analysis and parameter refinement. The implementation aims to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of sentiment detection, addressing the limitations of conventional approaches. The study explores the benefits of this approach in various scenarios and demonstrates its effectiveness through quantitative analysis.

title: Self-Organizing Neural Networks for Hardware Architecture Design
abstract: The design of neural network architectures for hardware implementation presents a significant challenge, often requiring substantial manual effort and specialized knowledge. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing a self-organizing neural network (SONN) to autonomously generate efficient neural network architectures tailored to specific hardware constraints. The SONN learns the design process directly from training data, iteratively evolving its own architecture based on performance metrics such as latency, power consumption, and accuracy. The core mechanism involves a recurrent neural network architecture, where each layer represents a design decision – e.g., layer type, number of neurons, connectivity patterns. The network is trained to minimize a cost function that combines these performance metrics with a regularization term encouraging architectural diversity. This approach offers a potentially automated and scalable solution for hardware architecture design, reducing the reliance on human expertise and accelerating the development of optimized neural network implementations. The paper details the architecture of the SONN, the training methodology, and presents a preliminary evaluation demonstrating the network's ability to generate architectures competitive with manually designed ones.

abstract: This paper explores the application of topology-driven design principles to quantum circuit design, aiming to enhance both quantum computation and quantum communication capabilities. We introduce a novel methodology leveraging topological structures to optimize circuit construction, leading to improved efficiency and performance. The core mechanism focuses on systematically incorporating topological constraints into the circuit design process, resulting in more robust and adaptable quantum circuits. The study begins with a foundational understanding of topological phases and their relevance to quantum information. We then detail a specific design framework incorporating these principles, demonstrating its effectiveness through a series of representative quantum circuit examples. The results showcase a significant improvement in quantum circuit performance compared to traditional approaches.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Natural Language Understanding
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to natural language understanding (NLU) that combines the strengths of neural networks and symbolic reasoning. Current deep learning models, while achieving impressive results in tasks like machine translation and question answering, often suffer from a lack of explainability and struggle with complex reasoning. We propose a neuro-symbolic framework where neural networks are used for perception and initial understanding, while symbolic reasoning techniques handle the logical inference and deduction required for more sophisticated tasks. This integration aims to overcome the limitations of purely data-driven approaches by injecting explicit knowledge and reasoning rules. The core claim of this work is that by merging the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks with the logical precision of symbolic systems, a more robust, explainable, and truly intelligent NLU system can be achieved. The proposed system is evaluated through a theoretical analysis of its components and potential applications, demonstrating its promise for tackling challenging NLU problems. We outline a key mechanism for achieving this integration and highlight the novel aspects of this combined approach.

title: Automatic classification of cyber incidents using privacy-preserving artificial intelligence
abstract: As cyber incidents increase in complexity, diversity and frequency, cybersecurity practitioners find it more challenging to extract meaningful threat intelligence and insights from cyber incident reports. This problem is worsened by the limited number of these reports; as cyber incident victims may withhold and/or downplaytheir reports due to reputational and privacy concerns. Therefore, this study aims to determine whether cyber incident reports, which have been stripped of personal data (pseudonymised), can be classified according to the Spanish INCIBE Cyber Incident Taxonomy. Seven transformers (SecBERT, BERT, DistilBERT, BERTweet, SecRoBERTa, ALBERT, RoBERTa) and four traditional machine learning classifiers (Random Forest, Multinomial Naïve Bayes, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine, using two encoders - Bag of Words and Term Frequency - Inverse Document Frequency), were trained to classify cyber incidents which were pseudonymised using Data Masking, Data Tokenisation and Data Substitution. The best-performing model attained an F1-score of 78.5% on the non-pseudonymised CECILIA-10C-900 dataset and 83% on the dataset, which was pseudonymised using Data Masking, D-CECILIA-10C-900-MAS. Therefore, this research demonstrates that it is possible for a single AI model to balance enhanced privacy with strong threat intelligence analysis capabilities.

title: Graph-based density-variation outlier removal for chronic disease prediction: A leakage-free benchmark and component-wise ablation
abstract: Chronic diseases such as diabetes, hypertension, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and heart disease impose a major global health burden. Machine-learning prediction systems offer valuable early-diagnostic support, but their performance is often degraded by outliers and class imbalance in real-world clinical tabular data. The standard remedy, DBSCAN, requires manual ε-tuning and assumes globally uniform density — assumptions that rarely hold on heterogeneous medical data. The recent AutoSCAN method removes the manual ε but has been validated only on synthetic clustering benchmarks, not on downstream medical classification. We propose YadroSeg, an extension of the graph-based coring framework of Le et al. [ 1 ], originally introduced for image segmentation, and adapted here to tabular medical data. YadroSeg builds a k-nearest-neighbour weighted graph and analyses a heap-based density variation sequence to identify noisy samples in an adaptive, parameter-free manner, using a novel geometric elbow criterion for automatic threshold selection. The cleaned data are then balanced with SMOTE-ENN and classified by a Random Forest. On five public chronic-disease datasets — diabetes, hypertension, CKD, Cleveland and Statlog heart disease — under 10-fold cross-validation, YadroSeg attains the best F1 on three datasets, reaching 98.87%. On the remaining two, YadroSeg-Grid and AutoSCAN are best, the latter benefiting from full data retention combined with SMOTE-ENN. These results confirm that graph-theoretic density analysis provides a mathematically principled and practically effective approach to noise filtering in imbalanced clinical tabular data.

title: Deep learning from the crowd Fundamentals of morphological galaxy classification
abstract: Aims. The objective of this work is to adapt a deep neural network model to perform galaxy morphological classification trained from crowd annotations, considering the training scheme, the agreement between the annotators, and the hierarchy. Methods. We use Galaxy Zoo 1 as our experimental testbed and trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) for the automatic classification of galaxies' morphologies. We analyze the impact of the following aspects on the classification accuracy and training efficiency: (i) Training only the last layer vs. training all the network; (ii) Classification with only the CNN vs. considering the hierarchy; (iii) Comparing the models trained with different amounts of data and levels of agreement between the annotators; (iv) Training by stages, transferring knowledge from one model to another; and (v) Combining several models as an ensemble. Results From the experiments, we derive the following results: (i) Training all the layers in the network significantly improves the accuracy (10% increase in exact match), compared to training only the last layer; (ii) There is a tradeoff between the amount of data and the level of agreement between the annotators used for training; (iii) Using the hierarchy can improve accuracy when the amount of training data is reduced; (iv) Training by stages through transfer learning (curriculum learning) produces higher accuracy for limited data; (v) Ensembles can improve accuracy; (vi) Models achieve a low accuracy for the most difficult cases, but, if we consider hierarchical measures, we can derive useful results for upper levels in the hierarchy. An accuracy above 99% is achieved when training all layers of the network and considering a high agreement between the annotators. Conclusions. Training deep learning models from crowd annotations involves additional challenges than learning from hard annotations.

title: LogicSkills: A Structured Benchmark for Formal Reasoning in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models perform well on many logical reasoning benchmarks, but it remains unclear which core logical skills they truly master. To address this, we introduce LogicSkills, a benchmark that isolates three fundamental logical skills: (i) formal symbolizationx2014{}translating premises into first-order logic; (ii) countermodel constructionx2014showing that an argument is logically invalid by constructing a finite countermodel; and (iii) validity assessmentx2014determining whether a conclusion follows from a set of premises. Items are drawn from the two-variable fragment of first-order logic without identity and are presented in both English and a Carrollian nonce-word language. All instances are solver-verified with Z3 for correctness and non-triviality. Across conventional instruction-tuned LLMs, performance is high on validity assessment but substantially lower on formal symbolization and countermodel construction, highlighting that high task-level accuracy can mask weaknesses in core logical skills. In contrast, recent reasoning-tuned models perform strongly across all three tasks, suggesting a more systematic logical skill profile.

title: The Adaptive Learning Framework Based on Graph-Based Machine Learning
abstract: This paper presents an adaptive learning framework for machine learning that automatically adjusts model parameters to enhance model performance. Traditional machine learning methods often lack the ability to dynamically adjust parameters based on data, limiting their effectiveness. This work introduces a novel approach leveraging graph structure to intelligently optimize model parameters, leading to improved accuracy and generalization. The framework employs a hierarchical graph representation to capture complex relationships within the data, facilitating automated parameter tuning. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through extensive experiments on various datasets, showcasing significant improvements in model performance compared to traditional methods. The core mechanism lies in the utilization of graph-based optimization techniques to systematically refine parameter values.

title: Quantum Entanglement Analysis and Anti-Decoy Algorithm
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a unique challenge to classical physics and has captivated researchers for decades. This paper investigates the concept of non-locality, specifically its connection to entanglement, and proposes a novel framework for analyzing quantum entanglement through a process called "Entanglement Anti-Decoy" (EAD). The core aim is to design an algorithm capable of reverse entanglement, offering a potential path towards quantum information processing. This research explores the implications of this approach, highlighting its potential to overcome the limitations of traditional quantum computation and provide a new avenue for exploring the mysteries of quantum entanglement. We will detail the proposed EAD algorithm, its underlying mathematical principles, and its potential to facilitate the development of robust quantum communication protocols. The paper will conclude with a discussion of the challenges and future directions for this research.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Phase Field Modeling
abstract: Quantum-enhanced phase field modeling presents a novel approach to predicting the behavior of materials under thermal and mechanical stress, aiming to significantly improve the accuracy of simulations compared to traditional methods. This paper details a new algorithmic framework leveraging quantum computation to accelerate the solution of phase field equations, addressing the computational bottleneck inherent in this modeling discipline. We explore the potential of quantum-enhanced iterative solvers to achieve substantial speedups and improved precision, ultimately offering a pathway toward more efficient and reliable material characterization. This work presents a rigorous theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation demonstrating the efficacy of this methodology.

title: Title: Non-Local Topological Field Theory (NTFT)
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for non-local topological field theory, aiming to overcome limitations in current quantum entanglement models. Traditional entanglement concepts often struggle with long-range effects, hindering the development of robust quantum information processing. NTFT proposes a radical shift, introducing a 'topological field' that facilitates instantaneous information transmission across distances, fundamentally altering the landscape of quantum computation. We explore the theoretical implications of this approach, detailing the core mechanism of information transfer and outlining a preliminary model for its application. The proposed theory offers a potential pathway to achieve truly global quantum information processing, exceeding the capabilities of conventional entanglement techniques.

title: Title: Zero-Assisted Geometric Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel zero-assistance geometric optimization algorithm designed to overcome the limitations of traditional optimization techniques, particularly in the presence of complex, high-dimensional search spaces. The core concept revolves around incorporating a probabilistic exploration strategy that allows the algorithm to escape local minima and discover optimal solutions even in regions classically considered inaccessible. We propose a mechanism that iteratively assesses the "assistance" required to continue exploration, dynamically adjusting the level of support to achieve efficient convergence. The algorithm's performance is evaluated across a range of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating a significant improvement in solution quality and efficiency compared to established methods. This work contributes to the advancement of geometric optimization and offers a new pathway for tackling challenging optimization problems.

title: Active Learning-based Machine Learning Model Training
abstract: This paper investigates the application of active learning techniques to enhance the training efficiency and accuracy of machine learning models. Traditional machine learning model training frequently relies on random sample selection, which can be highly inefficient, particularly when dealing with large datasets where the majority of data points may not contribute significantly to model improvement. Active learning provides a framework for intelligently selecting the most informative samples for annotation, thereby reducing the annotation burden while maximizing model performance. The core claim of this work is that by strategically utilizing active learning methods to prioritize sample selection based on uncertainty or information gain, we can significantly improve the training efficiency and overall predictive accuracy of machine learning models. We propose a novel active learning strategy based on model uncertainty quantification and information gain estimation. This approach aims to identify samples where the model is most uncertain or where labeling would provide the greatest information for model refinement. The methodology utilizes a core mechanism of constructing an active learning policy, offering a targeted approach to annotation, ultimately leading to more effective model training.

abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for intelligent system design centered around cognitive architectures. The framework aims to move beyond traditional rule-based or data-driven approaches by incorporating the nuanced and flexible nature of human cognition, ultimately resulting in systems that can better interact with and understand complex environments. title: HE-CloudML: a privacy-preserving framework for secure machine learning inference over encrypted cloud data using homomorphic encryption
abstract: Abstract The widespread adoption of cloud-based Machine Learning as a Service (MLaaS) exposes sensitive user data to critical privacy risks during inference, as plaintext data must typically be processed by untrusted cloud servers. This paper presents HE-CloudML, a unified privacy-preserving framework for secure deep neural network (DNN) inference over encrypted cloud data using Homomorphic Encryption (HE). HE-CloudML is architected as a three-tier system comprising a client-side CKKS encryption module, a cloud-side HE inference engine, and a distributed key management layer, ensuring that raw input data is never exposed to the server at any stage of computation. The framework introduces HE-compatible polynomial activation function approximations via degree-5 Chebyshev minimax polynomials, an optimized SIMD ciphertext batching strategy exploiting Ring Learning With Errors (RLWE) slot packing, and an adaptive lazy bootstrapping pipeline to substantially reduce homomorphic evaluation depth and inference latency. A formal security analysis under the IND-CPA model grounded in the RLWE hardness assumption demonstrates resistance to inference, model inversion, and membership inference attacks. Comprehensive experiments across three domains benchmark image classification (MNIST: 99.28%, CIFAR-10: 90.37%), medical imaging (93.61%), and financial fraud detection (96.44%) demonstrate that HE-CloudML achieves near-plaintext accuracy with a maximum accuracy drop of 1.81%, while delivering up to 26.9× latency improvements over CryptoNets.

title: (How) Do MLLMs Report Bistable Images Like Humans?
abstract: Bistable images such as the duck-rabbit are classic stimuli in which one image supports multiple mutually incompatible interpretations, typically reported one at a time in humans. We ask whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show similar report behavior and what internal computations support it. Using the LLaVA family, we study two tractable dimensions: modulability, whether reports can be biased by bottom-up visual cues and top-down linguistic priors, and exclusivity, whether responses commit to a single interpretation. We test both on the canonical duck-rabbit and on synthetic Visual Anagrams to mitigate memorization confounds. Behaviorally, both visual and linguistic manipulations systematically shift reports in human-consistent ways, while responses remain predominantly exclusive. Mechanistically, these effects arise from competing image-token representations, distinct pathways for bottom-up and top-down modulation, and a link between exclusive reporting and object-count encoding. Code and data are available at https://github.com/rtakatsky/mllm-bistable-images.

title: Efficient Hardware Information-Flow Tracking for Pre-Silicon Security Testing
abstract: Register-Transfer Level (RTL) simulation is widely used to test hardware before it is fabricated. To allow testing for security related information flow properties, such as confidentiality and integrity, taint logic can be automatically added to the design to track how information flows through it. However, taint logic instrumented by the state-of-the-art, such as CellIFT, makes simulation-based testing prohibitively expensive: On our evaluation of Mega-BOOM (136K cells), it increases the instrumented design to 5.81x the original cell count and causes a 143.72x simulation slowdown. The taint logic could be simplified to improve simulation speed, but it will inevitably trade off its precision. This lightweight, imprecise taint logic will introduce false positives and may eventually result in even more overhead to check these false positives. This paper explores the research question of where precision is actually needed in the design to overcome the overhead of false positives. It presents CEGAR-T, a framework that automatically synthesizes taint logic that minimizes the taint-logic instrumentation overhead while guaranteeing no false positives (relative to the precise CellIFT baseline). We have implemented CEGAR-T and evaluated it on the safe instruction set problem for timing side-channel security across open-source RISC-V cores. Over all evaluated cores, CEGAR-T reduces both instrumentation and simulation overhead, in geometric-mean, from 5.64x to 1.42x and from 34.65x to 1.79x, respectively, without compromising the precision benefit of the CellIFT baseline.

title: Reading Decoder Trajectories: Training-Free Counterfactual Query-Trajectory Reliability for Small-Object Detection
abstract: Small-object detection remains challenging because limited pixels cause information loss and suppress the scale knowledge encoded in pretrained detectors. Existing approaches mainly improve representations through multiscale training, architecture redesign, or parameter adaptation, implicitly assuming that frozen models lack the required capability. We challenge this assumption and hypothesize that small-object knowledge already exists in frozen detectors but remains underactivated and unstable during query evolution. To test this hypothesis, we propose Counterfactual Query-Trajectory Reliability (CQTR), a training-free framework that elicits latent responses through counterfactual scale interventions and interprets candidate reliability from decoder-internal spatial convergence, semantic persistence, and cross-scale conflicts. A small unlabeled training subset selects the appropriate correction mechanism for each model-data stream, without parameter updates or target-domain annotations. Across 27 combinations of nine frozen detectors and three datasets, CQTR consistently improves average precision (AP) and average precision for small objects (APs). Closed-loop analyses further show that scale intervention activates latent responses, trajectory evidence predicts ground-truth support, and unlabeled routing selects the more effective branch. CQTR therefore reframes small-object detection from external scale augmentation to the activation and reliability assessment of latent scale knowledge.

title: Title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Universal Computation Model
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a phenomenon where two or more particles become linked and share the same fate no matter how far apart they are, has emerged as a potentially transformative force in quantum computing. This paper explores the feasibility of utilizing quantum entanglement as a core mechanism for creating a universal computational model, capable of tackling complex calculations across diverse quantum systems. We propose a novel approach that leverages entanglement to establish a fundamentally different computational paradigm, moving beyond the limitations of classical computation. The core claim of this research is that a well-designed quantum entanglement-based computational framework can enable computations that are fundamentally impossible for classical computers. This work details the proposed model, its underlying principles, and potential applications across various computational domains.

title: Quantum Entanglement Computing Optimization via Nonlinear Models
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a unique opportunity for computation exceeding the capabilities of classical systems. This work addresses a critical challenge in quantum computing, focusing on the potential of non-linear models to unlock new optimization strategies.

title: Rank Aware Strategic Policy Design for Language Based Economic Environments
abstract: Games in Language Based Economic Environments (GLEE) evaluates language agents in multiround bargaining, bilateral negotiation, and repeated persuasion. We report an agent that finished second in the 2026 agent track at a rating of 2590.02 after 46,564 officially rated games. Because GLEE ranks payoffs within each configuration and role, maximizing expected money need not maximize the competition score. Our final policy combines game-theoretic benchmarks, fitted opponent-response models, and history-based rules without a language model at inference. Bargaining balances discounted continuation against agreement risk; negotiation separates visible-surplus decisions from hidden-value inference; persuasion uses recommendations, observed quality, and credibility to guide purchases. We trace the development and failures of these strategies. A separate 245-game final-policy audit connects 2,288 returned actions to authenticated replays. Agreement alone was insufficient: all 15 bargaining games in which a rank-proxy rule changed offers agreed, yet 14 lost rating. These results describe a competitive system, not individual component effects.

abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic algorithm design based on adaptive probability distributions. The core idea is to dynamically adjust the probability distribution parameters of an optimization algorithm based on observed data from the environment. This adaptive approach allows the algorithm to learn and optimize more efficiently, offering enhanced robustness and adaptability to changing conditions. The proposed method significantly improves the performance of optimization tasks compared to traditional methods.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Theory: An Adaptive Gaussian Field Theory
abstract: Quantum entanglement is a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, exhibiting correlations that defy classical intuition. This research investigates the use of an adaptive Gaussian field theory to construct a robust model for quantum entanglement information theory. This model aims to provide more accurate simulations of entanglement properties and precise measurement/control capabilities, particularly within the context of quantum computing and quantum communication. The core mechanism involves integrating Gaussian field theory with the mathematical description of entanglement, allowing for dynamic adaptation of the entanglement state to environmental fluctuations. This approach offers a significant advancement in our understanding and manipulation of quantum entanglement. The paper demonstrates the model's ability to capture complex entanglement behaviors and provides a framework for advanced quantum algorithms and secure communication protocols.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Satisfaction (QECS)
abstract: This paper introduces Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Satisfaction (QECS), a novel algorithm designed to accelerate the solution of complex optimization problems using quantum annealing. Traditional constraint satisfaction algorithms often struggle with large, high-dimensional search spaces, limiting their effectiveness. QECS leverages quantum annealing to efficiently explore the solution space, potentially offering exponential speedups compared to classical methods. The core mechanism centers on using quantum annealing to identify and exploit local optima, significantly reducing the computational cost of finding optimal solutions. We present a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance, demonstrating its potential for substantial improvements in optimization tasks across diverse problem domains.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Programming with Bayesian Knowledge Graphs
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to programming – Neuro-Symbolic Programming with Bayesian Knowledge Graphs (KNP) – designed to overcome the limitations of traditional neural networks and symbolic AI systems. The core idea is to create a synergistic system that leverages the pattern recognition abilities of neural networks and the logical deduction capabilities of symbolic reasoning, mediated by a Bayesian Knowledge Graph. The system learns to translate raw data into symbolic representations, which are then utilized within the KGP for probabilistic inference and the generation of executable symbolic programs. This iterative process continuously refines both the neural representation and the underlying symbolic knowledge, leading to a dynamically adapting reasoning engine. We present a detailed framework for the KNP, emphasizing the Bayesian component and its role in enabling robust and flexible programming. The system's architecture, incorporating a neural network for feature extraction and a Bayesian Knowledge Graph for inference and program generation, represents a significant advancement in the field of neuro-symbolic AI. Ultimately, this work demonstrates a pathway towards more intelligent and adaptable AI systems capable of handling complex, real-world problems.

title: Explainable AI via Causal Mediation Analysis of Neural Network Predictions
abstract: The increasing deployment of neural networks in critical applications necessitates methods for understanding their decision-making processes – a field often referred to as Explainable AI (XAI). Traditional XAI techniques frequently provide post-hoc explanations that lack a solid causal foundation, potentially masking spurious correlations and leading to misleading interpretations. This paper proposes a novel approach to XAI that leverages causal mediation analysis to uncover the underlying causal pathways driving neural network predictions. We treat the neural network's prediction as a mediator variable, allowing us to rigorously assess the relationships between input features and the target variable through this intermediary. This framework provides a more robust and interpretable explanation by explicitly considering causal mechanisms. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical exploration and illustrate its benefits with a simplified example. The core claim of this work is that causal mediation analysis significantly enhances the explainability of neural network predictions by revealing the true causal influences.

title: Quantum Computing Adaptive Parameter Adjustment Algorithm
abstract: Quantum computing offers unprecedented computational power, but realizing this potential requires sophisticated algorithms for parameter optimization. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with the inherent complexities of quantum systems, particularly when dealing with large, multi-dimensional parameter spaces. This paper introduces a novel quantum computing algorithm, the Quantum Parameter Adjustment Algorithm (QPAA), designed to address these challenges by dynamically analyzing quantum process to automatically adjust parameters, thereby enhancing both computational efficiency and accuracy. This algorithm leverages machine learning techniques to achieve self-adaptive parameter correction, offering a fundamentally new approach to quantum optimization. We provide a detailed explanation of the algorithm's core mechanisms, including the dynamic analysis framework and the machine learning component, and discuss the potential benefits and limitations of this approach.

title: #基于生物神经网络的自适应控制系统 (BNAC)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel Adaptive Control System based on Biological Neural Networks (BNAC), aiming to address the limitations of conventional control systems regarding adaptability and robustness. The core concept of BNAC lies in mimicking the self-organizing capabilities observed in biological neural networks. Specifically, we leverage a Pulse Neural Network (PNN) architecture and utilize synaptic plasticity – the ability of synapses to strengthen or weaken over time – to enable adaptive control strategies. This approach allows the system to dynamically adjust its control parameters in response to changes in the environment. Mathematical formulations are presented to detail the PNN model and the plasticity rules. The key novelty of BNAC resides in its direct emulation of biological neural network adaptation, promising enhanced resilience and performance in complex control scenarios. We demonstrate the theoretical framework and outline a potential implementation strategy for BNAC systems.

title: Neural Evolution Network (NEN)
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network design and optimization, termed the Neural Evolution Network (NEN). The core concept of NEN involves integrating the principles of neural networks with evolutionary algorithms, specifically utilizing a genetic algorithm to dynamically optimize both the network's architecture and the connections between neurons. Traditional methods for neural network design often rely on manual tuning and expert knowledge, leading to suboptimal performance. NEN addresses this limitation by introducing a self-adaptive evolutionary process. The algorithm iteratively modifies the network's structure and weights based on its performance, enabling the network to evolve towards solutions that are better suited to the given task. The key mechanism involves evaluating network performance, generating variations through genetic operators (mutation, crossover), and selecting the most promising individuals for the next generation. This process continues until a satisfactory solution is achieved or a predefined stopping criterion is met. The resulting NEN demonstrates improved adaptability and potentially superior performance compared to networks designed through conventional methods.

title: Algorithmic Stability Analysis via Abstract Interpretation
abstract: Algorithmic stability analysis in distributed systems is a critical aspect of ensuring correct and reliable operation, particularly as systems grow in complexity and scale. However, traditional methods for assessing stability – often relying on exhaustive simulation – quickly become computationally infeasible due to the exponential growth of possible system states. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging abstract interpretation techniques to address this challenge. We demonstrate how abstract models can be derived from distributed algorithms, enabling efficient analysis of stability properties without the need for full-scale simulations. Our methodology provides a scalable solution for analyzing algorithmic stability, offering a significant advancement over existing approaches. The core claim is that analyzing algorithmic stability is computationally intractable. The core mechanism involves applying abstract interpretation to derive abstract models, facilitating efficient stability analysis. This approach represents a new way to tackle the problem, offering a scalable solution.

title: Adaptive Algorithm Based on Bioelectrochemical Feedback
abstract: This paper explores the development and implementation of an adaptive algorithm leveraging bioelectrochemical feedback for improved performance. The core concept involves utilizing real-time physiological signals, such as electroencephalogram (EEG) and electrocardiogram (ECG), as feedback to dynamically adjust algorithm parameters and strategies. This approach moves beyond traditional, static optimization methods by incorporating the inherent dynamics of biological systems. The proposed methodology employs adaptive optimization algorithms, including genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization, to fine-tune algorithm parameters based on the analyzed biofeedback signals. We establish a mapping between bioelectrical signal characteristics and algorithm performance, enabling a truly adaptive and intelligent system. The research highlights the potential for creating more robust and responsive algorithms across diverse applications where real-time adaptation is crucial.

title: Geometric Topology and Quantum Computing: A Convergence
abstract: This paper explores the synergistic convergence of geometric topology and quantum computing. We investigate the potential for utilizing quantum computing's inherent parallelism to accelerate and enhance geometric topology computations, specifically focusing on verification and novel exploration of topological properties. The core mechanism involves employing quantum algorithms to perform computationally intensive geometric analysis, coupled with the quantum computer's ability to detect subtle topological variations. The paper presents a framework for investigating the interplay between these two fields, highlighting the potential for groundbreaking discoveries. The research aims to reveal deeper geometric insights through the combined power of quantum computation and mathematical analysis.

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization of Large-Scale Machine Learning Models
abstract: The training of large-scale machine learning models presents significant computational challenges, primarily due to the inherent complexity of optimization algorithms like stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants. These algorithms often struggle with convergence speed, getting trapped in local minima, and the ability to effectively explore the vast solution space. This paper investigates the potential of quantum-inspired optimization techniques to address these limitations. Specifically, we explore the application of quantum annealing and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) approaches to accelerate the training and optimization process of large-scale machine learning models. Our core claim is that by mapping the optimization problem to a quantum system, we can leverage quantum computation to overcome the computational bottlenecks associated with classical optimization methods. We propose a framework where the objective function of the machine learning model is translated into a Hamiltonian for a quantum annealer or the cost function for a VQE, enabling a quantum-inspired solution. The results, while theoretical in this initial exploration, demonstrate a potential pathway for significantly reducing training times and improving the overall performance of large-scale machine learning models. Further research is needed to develop efficient hybrid quantum-classical algorithms and explore the practical limitations of this approach.

title: Explainable Deep Learning Models: Leveraging Causal Inference for Enhanced Interpretability and Reliability
abstract: This paper investigates the application of causal inference techniques to enhance the interpretability and reliability of deep learning models. Traditional deep learning models often operate as black boxes, lacking transparency and making it difficult to understand the reasoning behind their predictions. We propose a framework that integrates causal reasoning into the model architecture and inference process. This framework aims to identify and utilize the underlying causal relationships within the data and model, thereby providing more meaningful and trustworthy explanations. Specifically, we explore methods for detecting spurious correlations and disentangling causal influences. The core claim of this research is that leveraging causal inference significantly improves both the interpretability and the robustness of deep learning models. Our approach offers a pathway towards building more reliable and trustworthy AI systems, addressing a critical limitation of current deep learning technology. The presented methodology provides a structured approach for incorporating causal reasoning, ultimately leading to models that are not only accurate but also explainable.

title: Organization of Valence and Arousal in Vision-Language Representations of Built Environments: Insights from the EMOIS Dataset
abstract: Visual perception of built environments contributes to the affective impressions that people form in everyday life. However, how these impressions are represented within vision foundation models remains largely unexplored. To support the systematic investigation of this subject, we introduce the Emotional Impression of Spaces (EMOIS) dataset, comprising 1,544 real-world built-environment images. Each image is annotated with image-evoked valence and arousal ratings collected from Japanese adults by conducting a large-scale web-based survey, with approximately 120 ratings per image. Using Contrastive Language--Image Pre-training (CLIP) representations, we perform predictive and geometric analyses to systematically investigate how valence and arousal are encoded and organized within the representation space. These analyses reveal that valence exhibited stronger and more coherent organization than arousal. Cross-dataset analyses with the Open Affective Standardized Image Set (OASIS), a benchmark dataset of general affective photographs, reveal differences in affective organization between the two datasets. Regression analyses demonstrate high predictive performance for valence and arousal within EMOIS, with mean coefficients of determination of 0.865 and 0.807, respectively, across repeated internal hold-out evaluations. Finally, we present an example-based interface illustrating how learned representations can support qualitative interpretation of predicted affective values. These findings can help elucidate affective representations of built environments and establish EMOIS as a densely annotated resource for future affective computing research in this domain.

title: Computation and Applications of Euclidean and Normed Representations of Massive Data
abstract: This thesis investigates Euclidean-space and $\ell_p$-norm representations of different forms of data, with a focus on efficient algorithms for computing these representations in settings where the amount of data is very large. The applications of such representations are also discussed: they may be used to summarize the data in a more compact form for downstream tasks while preserving its most salient properties; and further, they may also be used to extract insights about the data that may not be apparent in its original form. This thesis presents novel algorithms for computing Euclidean representations in the case where the data comes with linear structure, as well as in the case where the data comes only with metric, or distance structure. In addition, we give algorithms for computing $\ell_p$-norm representations in linear structured cases. The analyses of these algorithms use tools from geometry, probability, and optimization, and these tools are used to illuminate other algorithms for similar problems.

title: Reliability, validity, and diagnostic evidence for multi-model LLM short-answer scoring
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used or proposed for educational scoring, but single-model and single-run evaluations provide limited evidence for assessment use. Short-answer scoring requires evidence about reliability, validity, severity, diagnostic value, and failure cases. This study evaluated repeated multi-model OCG-PRES guided LLM scoring for short-answer assessment. The analysis used 996 SciEntsBank responses. GPT, DeepSeek, and Qianwen each scored every response across three independent runs using five OCG-PRES dimensions: concept coverage, relation accuracy, reasoning completeness, contradiction control, and domain relevance. Scores were evaluated against official binary and five-category labels and compared with non-LLM baselines based on answer length, Jaccard keyword overlap, TF-IDF cosine similarity, and a combined traditional logistic model. Repeated-run reliability was high for all models, with ICC(3,k) = .977 for GPT, .992 for DeepSeek, and .981 for Qianwen. DeepSeek was the most stable across runs. GPT showed the strongest official-label alignment by AUC (.909), while Qianwen was stricter, with higher precision but lower recall under the fixed threshold = 3.0 rule. OCG-PRES scores followed expected diagnostic patterns across five official categories and outperformed all non-LLM baselines in AUC and F1. Repeated multi-model OCG-PRES scoring provides reliability, validity, and diagnostic evidence for LLM-assisted short-answer scoring. The findings support cautious, evidence-based use as a scoring support tool rather than a replacement for human judgement.

title: The Adaptive Optimization of Algorithmic Parameter Tuning via Graph-Based Adaptation
abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive optimization algorithm for algorithmic parameter tuning, leveraging the power of graph-based adaptation. The core innovation lies in utilizing a graph structure to automatically adjust algorithm parameters, significantly enhancing the algorithm's adaptability and performance across diverse datasets and problem domains. The algorithm's architecture is designed to dynamically adjust parameters based on observed data patterns, resulting in improved convergence speed, robustness, and generalization capabilities. This work lays the groundwork for future research in utilizing quantum systems for time series analysis and prediction, offering a potential pathway to overcome limitations of conventional approaches.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks for Quantum State Preparation
abstract: Quantum state preparation is a fundamental and often rate-limiting step in many quantum information processing tasks, including quantum computation, quantum communication, and quantum metrology. Traditional methods for preparing complex quantum states rely on iterative techniques, which can be computationally expensive and time-consuming. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to directly generate complex quantum states from classical inputs. The core idea is to train a GAN to learn the probability distribution of quantum states, effectively learning a mapping between classical data and corresponding quantum states. We formulate the problem as a minimax game between a generator and a discriminator, where the generator aims to produce realistic quantum states, and the discriminator aims to distinguish between generated and real quantum states. The mathematical formulation of this process is detailed below. We hypothesize that this approach will offer significant speedups compared to traditional state preparation methods, particularly for complex states. The success of this approach hinges on the ability of the GAN to accurately capture the intricate correlations inherent in quantum state distributions. This work provides a foundational framework for exploring the application of GANs in quantum state preparation and lays the groundwork for future research in this area.

title: Neuro-Graph Adaptive Optimization (NGAO)
abstract: This paper introduces Neuro-Graph Adaptive Optimization (NGAO), a novel approach to neural network optimization that leverages graph neural networks (GNNs) and reinforcement learning (RL) to achieve adaptive learning and generalization. The core claim of NGAO is that by dynamically adjusting the connection strengths and topology of a neural network, it can better adapt to evolving input data distributions, leading to improved efficiency and performance. NGAO operates by first using a GNN to analyze the current input data distribution represented as a graph, identifying optimization targets such as connection strength adjustments or node additions/deletions. Subsequently, a reinforcement learning agent, employing a policy gradient method, dynamically adjusts the network's connections and topology to maximize a reward signal, typically related to prediction accuracy or energy consumption. This iterative optimization process results in a neural network graph structure that more accurately reflects the current data distribution, ultimately enhancing performance. NGAO's key innovation lies in treating the neural network as a graph and utilizing GNNs and RL in a synergistic manner to enable adaptive optimization, particularly for non-static, dynamic data distributions, and proactive topological changes.

title: Dynamical System Representation of Neural Network Dynamics
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to understanding and manipulating neural network dynamics by framing them as complex dynamical systems. We argue that neural networks, despite their complex architecture and training processes, exhibit behaviors that can be rigorously analyzed using the established tools of chaos theory and dynamical systems analysis. Specifically, we map the activation dynamics of a neural network onto a state-space representation, utilizing techniques such as Lyapunov exponents, bifurcation analysis, and Poincaré sections to characterize the system's behavior. The core contribution lies in demonstrating that the inherent complexities within neural networks – often considered solely as a result of training – can be attributed to underlying dynamical structures, potentially exhibiting chaotic behavior. This shift in perspective offers new avenues for enhancing network robustness, designing controlled transitions, and ultimately, achieving more predictable and reliable network performance. This work provides a theoretical framework for understanding and potentially controlling neural network dynamics, moving beyond traditional black-box training methodologies. ---

title: Dynamic Bayesian Networks for Real-Time Anomaly Detection in Sensor Data
abstract: This paper explores the application of Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) for real-time anomaly detection in sensor data. Traditional anomaly detection methods often rely on static thresholds or rule-based systems, which are ineffective when dealing with complex, time-varying systems. DBNs offer a powerful alternative by explicitly modeling the temporal dependencies within the sensor data and learning the underlying system dynamics. The proposed approach constructs a DBN that represents the relationships between sensor readings and system states, continuously updating its model based on incoming data. Anomalies are identified as deviations from the learned model, enabling proactive detection and response. The core claim is that DBNs can accurately detect anomalies in real-time sensor data by learning the underlying system dynamics and identifying deviations from expected behavior. This research presents a novel methodology for real-time anomaly detection, providing a robust and adaptable solution for systems with dynamic behavior.

title: PPIM: Pennes Physics-Informed Mamba for Heat-Source-Conditioned 3D Bioheat Simulation
abstract: Three-dimensional bioheat simulation aims to predict transient temperature distributions in biological tissue and is commonly modeled using the Pennes bioheat equation, which combines thermal diffusion, perfusion-mediated heat loss, and external heat generation. In this study, we consider a controlled 3D Pennes bioheat simulation under a localized heat-source condition inspired by microwave ablation (MWA). To evaluate neural approximation performance, we compare three neural partial differential equation (PDE) solvers under the same controlled simulation: a spatial Fourier-feature physics-informed neural network (PINN), a generic PINNMamba temporal subsequence model, and Pennes Physics-Informed Mamba (PPIM). PPIM builds on the temporal subsequence model by incorporating conditioned heat-source input and Pennes-aware state-space model (SSM) decay initialization. All three neural models are trained under the same conditions with the same Pennes residual, and an explicit finite-difference method (FDM) solution is used only as the numerical reference. In a representative 600~s run, PPIM achieved the lowest MAE, relative $L_1$ error, and relative $L_2$ error among the evaluated neural solvers. Error maps further showed that the remaining PPIM errors were more concentrated near the heat-source region than across the rest of the domain. These results indicate that PPIM is effective for approximating the FDM reference final temperature field in this controlled simulation. The source code is available at https://github.com/muvYun/PPIM.

title: A TTP by TTP Approach: Precise Malware Detection via Malicious TTP Recognition
abstract: Machine learning methods, and especially neural networks, are now routinely used for malware detection in network traffic. Though very effective, systems based on such methods often (i) are purely data-driven, ignoring the substantial body of available knowledge about the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) possibly used, and, consequently (ii) are not precise, since they either cannot correlate malicious activity with TTP usage, or if they do, they are unable to explain which TTP has been maliciously used. In this paper we demonstrate that it is possible to precisely detect malware by (i) providing the neural network model with information about the TTPs used by any given sample, and (ii) teaching the neural network to detect not just the malicious activity as a whole, but which specific TTPs are maliciously used. We show that our approach consistently outperforms the three alternative models, which either do not exploit TTP information, or which are not taught to detect the malicious usage of TTPs, or both. title: TransLearn: Representing and Comparing Transformer Architectures in a Free Categorical Framework
abstract: We define TransLearn, a free category of residual sequential architecture terms generated by a typed primitive signature. Its base doctrine is Cartesian with specified commutative-monoid operations on residual objects, rather than biproducts, so nonlinear Euclidean layers remain admissible. For a fixed signature, finite-graph completeness identifies the terms with finite acyclic typed architecture graphs modulo the stated Cartesian, monoid, and sequence-coherence equations; pure signature extensions are conservative on old terms. The syntax separates parameter identity, runtime routing, causality, state, and implementation labels. Finite depth-sharing patterns form the partition lattice; nested routed families flatten to a single routed family when dispatch and combine morphisms are unrestricted; and support certificates give a sufficient prefix-causality test for length-changing residual branches. Applied to Funnel-Transformer's published stride-2 mean pooling and repetition upsampling, the test leads to an explicit counterexample showing that their direct composition is noncausal if reused unchanged inside an autoregressive residual branch. The theory decides these structural questions; it does not decide optimization, accuracy, or hardware efficiency without additional interpretations or cost assumptions.

title: ViNoise-CSE: Contrastive Learning with Tone-Dropping Augmentation for Robust Vietnamese Text Classification
abstract: Vietnamese is a highly tonal language where the presence or absence of diacritics significantly alters word meanings. On social media, users often omit diacritics—either for typing convenience or to evade content moderation filters—which degrades the performance of standard NLP models. In this paper, we propose ViNoise-CSE, a contrastive learning framework that integrates a novel ToneDropper data augmentation strategy. By jointly training with tone-dropped positive pairs, ViNoise-CSE learns sentence representations that are resilient to diacritic omission. We evaluate our method on two downstream tasks: Hate Speech Detection (ViHSD) and Sentiment Analysis (VSFC). Experimental results show that the pure tone-dropping configuration of ViNoise-CSE significantly outperforms the strong PhoBERT baseline under extreme synthetic diacritic-loss conditions (+12.28% Macro-F1 at 100% tone dropping). Furthermore, the learned representations demonstrate exceptional stability, maintaining nearly flat performance across all noise levels (dropping only 1.49% F1 from 0% to 100% noise). Our semi-supervised variant (SupCon) substantially improves few-shot performance, yielding a +20.88% Macro-F1 gain over the baseline with only 1% labeled data. Finally, we provide a critical empirical evaluation showing that while contrastive pre-training excels in few-shot settings, simple supervised data augmentation outperforms it when full labeled datasets are available.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic geometric transformation constraint algorithm based on quantum entanglement. The core mechanism involves establishing entangled states to represent the transformation's state, allowing for a more nuanced and responsive adjustment of constraints.

This paper explores the algorithmic application of entanglement to propagate geometric information, aiming to facilitate the creation of intricate geometric structures and rigorous proofs of geometric theorems. The core mechanism centers around designing a "quantum map" – a state that utilizes entanglement to traverse geometric spaces, potentially enabling the generation of infinitely complex geometries. We present a novel algorithm that demonstrates the feasibility of this approach, highlighting its potential to revolutionize computational geometry and offer significant advancements in geometric analysis.

The algorithm's design incorporates a novel dynamic adjustment strategy, significantly improving the efficiency and scalability of quantum computation.

title: Title: Dynamic Quantum Error Mitigation through Entanglement Transfer
abstract: Quantum computing holds immense promise for solving complex problems currently intractable for classical computers. However, inherent quantum errors pose a significant barrier to this progress. This research investigates a novel dynamic quantum error mitigation technique leveraging entanglement transfer to actively correct errors during computation. Our work proposes a system where entangled states are continuously transferred between different parts of the quantum circuit, allowing for the 'correction' of errors through the manipulation of entanglement itself. The core mechanism centers around strategically transferring entanglement to minimize the impact of errors, leading to enhanced computational reliability. This approach moves beyond traditional reactive error mitigation strategies, offering a proactive and potentially transformative method for achieving high-fidelity quantum computations.

title: Quantum Bayesian Inference with Entangled Noise
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to Bayesian inference that exploits the inherent noise present in quantum systems. The core idea is to utilize entangled quantum systems to generate noise patterns exhibiting strong statistical correlations. These correlations, when measured, are then directly incorporated as prior probabilities within a Bayesian inference engine, leading to improved accuracy compared to traditional Bayesian methods relying solely on classical noise. The methodology moves beyond merely utilizing quantum randomness, actively harnessing the correlated information contained within quantum noise to reshape the inference process. We demonstrate, theoretically, the potential for significant improvements in model accuracy by strategically leveraging these correlations. The framework presented offers a promising avenue for enhancing Bayesian inference in complex scenarios, particularly where classical noise sources are limited in their ability to provide correlated information. The mathematical formalism presented outlines the key principles and equations governing this process.

title: Quantum Error Correction with Hybrid Dynamical Systems – Dynamical Optimization of Error Correction Codes
abstract: Quantum error correction is a critical challenge in quantum computing, demanding robust and efficient methods to mitigate errors that inevitably arise during computation. Traditional approaches often rely on fixed error correction codes, which struggle to adapt to the dynamic nature of quantum systems. This paper proposes a hybrid dynamical systems approach to quantum error correction, integrating established techniques with a dynamically adjustable system that optimizes error correction strategies. We demonstrate that this approach can significantly improve error correction performance compared to existing methods by leveraging the strengths of both traditional and adaptive techniques. The core mechanism involves a dynamic adjustment of the error correction strategy based on observed error characteristics, achieved through a hybrid dynamical system. This system continuously monitors the error profile and adjusts the correction parameters to achieve optimal performance. We present theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental results supporting this approach, highlighting its potential to advance the field of quantum error correction.

title: Spectral bounds for the partial transpose
abstract: Among the various entanglement measures, the negativity stands out not only for its clear physical meaning but also for being directly computable from the spectrum of the partial transpose. However, the negativity captures only the total weight of the negative eigenvalues, whereas the finer structure of the negative spectrum remains largely unexplored. In this work, we fill this gap by introducing a hierarchical generalization of the negativity, the Ky Fan $k$-negativity, and developing a unified analytical framework for deriving spectral bounds on the partial transpose. To obtain the absolute bounds, we reduce the maximization problem to a spectral graph optimization, whose solution yields the exact bound for every $k$ through a single cubic equation. We further investigate these spectral bounds both analytically and numerically under a fixed-purity constraint. In particular, we solve the $k=1$ case completely and uncover a simple underlying graph structure. As two direct applications, we show that the Ky Fan $k$-negativity robustly certifies genuine multilevel entanglement and that it converts the $p_3$-PPT condition into a quantitative lower bound on the negativity.
