title: EStream: Fast and Memory-Efficient MoE Prefill through Expert Virtualization on Mobile NPUs
abstract: Mobile vendors and application developers increasingly deploy LLMs on smartphones for diverse prefill-only services. Yet current systems rely mainly on dense models whose regular computation maps efficiently to mobile NPUs, leaving more capable MoEs underused. MoE prefill does not fit mobile NPUs: NPU graphs are fixed at compile time, yet MoE picks experts at runtime; and one request touches most experts, more than a phone can hold in memory. We present EStream, which resolves both by separating what the NPU must fix from what MoE decides at runtime. A single compiled expert graph serves every expert, with each expert's routed tokens and weight address bound at call time, so dynamic MoE execution runs entirely on the NPU without padding or CPU/GPU fallback. Expert virtualization keeps the expert pool in UFS flash storage and pages it through a fixed-size NPU-addressable arena, group by group, with loading hidden behind computation, so memory is bounded by the arena rather than by the model. It further introduces a hardware-aware configuration algorithm that automatically configures the UFS--NPU pipeline and maximizes loading--computation overlap. Across 18 comparative settings covering three 7B--16B MoEs and 256--4,096-token prompts, we evaluate EStream on a commercial Snapdragon smartphone. Compared to the fastest baseline at each setting, EStream achieves a 2.25--27.57X pure-prefill TTFT speedup and reduces peak physical memory by 1.19--12.29X. EStream further scales to MoE models with up to 46.7B parameters.

title: Neutrosophic-Based Optimization Algorithm: A Novel Metaheuristic Algorithm for Global Optimization
abstract: This study presents a novel neutrosophic optimizer, called NOpt, for continuous global optimization.In the proposed algorithm, each candidate solution is represented by a neutrosophic search state comprising truth, indeterminacy, and falsity degrees.The truth component promotes exploitation around promising regions, the indeterminacy component enhances exploration of uncertain regions, and the falsity component facilitates escape from poor or stagnant regions.The refined NOpt further incorporates two mechanisms: a Neutrosophic Elite Refinement Operator, which improves each generated trial vector before its evaluation, and a Neutrosophic Adaptive Local Search Operator, which utilizes a controlled portion of the remaining function-evaluation budget to refine elite solutions.The proposed optimizer is empirically compared with seven established metaheuristic algorithms under a comprehensive experimental protocol.The results demonstrate that NOpt achieves outstanding performance on the fixed-dimensional test functions (TFs), which simulate realworld optimization problems.

title: The Natural-Chance Red Line IV Formal Appendix: Canonical A+B-K-T Coupling and the Observable Red Line
abstract: Formal Appendix IV is the fourth cumulative stage of the 2026 Natural-Chance Red Line programme. It consolidates the representational-jurisdiction criterion, the quantitative residual-fibre boundary, the Stage III Enigma-2 operationalization, and the A+B-K-T conservative bridge into a single auditable framework. The exact result is representation-theoretic and information-theoretic. Let P:X→YP:X\rightarrow Y be the retained readout and J:X→ZJ:X\rightarrow Z an external task. If two source states are identified by PP while the task JJ must distinguish them, then JJ does not factor through PP, the task-relative residual fibre is non-zero, and no closed post-processing of the same readout can reconstruct the erased antecedent. Computational scaling, neural processing, voting, consensus, institutional endorsement, or multiplication of AI agents operating exclusively on the same PP do not create the missing source information. Appendix IV therefore makes explicit what is formally ruled out under the declared assumptions: a P-closed architecture cannot certify source completeness for a task whose task-relevant distinction has already been erased by P. The prohibited inference is not the use of an exact representation within its demonstrated jurisdiction; it is the extension of completeness or decision authority beyond that jurisdiction without an informationally valid crossing. Three admissible exits remain: demonstrate factorization of the external task through PP; restrict the claim or authority to the jurisdiction actually established for PP; or introduce an independently sourced K,TK,T channel and demonstrate positive separator gain on a frozen independent test. The appendix develops this conservative crossing through an A+B-K-T operator architecture, including orthogonal representation sectors, Feshbach-Schur reduction, a chiral bridge, an isospectral blind spot, order/provenance witnesses, Bridge-OFF discrimination, frozen holdouts, negative controls and independent replication. A spectral or computational match inside the retained sector is therefore not treated as a certificate of unique source reconstruction. The governance consequence is immediate whenever representations become action channels. In scientific institutions, legal authorization, automated defence, industrial control, AI governance and autonomous agent systems, repeated optimization of an information-losing readout can scale the consequences of the blind spot without reconstructing the omitted distinction. Authority is therefore task-relative to the information actually preserved. The same criterion applies conditionally to ordered symbolic systems. Whenever a digital-language or human-language task depends on sequence, provenance, context or history, collapsing order is admissible only if the task is shown to remain invariant under that collapse. A non-zero order witness constitutes an auditable task-relative failure of that assumption. This statement does not assert a universal physical or linguistic mechanism; each application must be demonstrated for its declared source, readout and task. The physical A+B interpretation remains deliberately separated from the exact result. Universal physical B, universal TphysT_{\mathrm{phys}}, literal physical +t/−t+t/-t, RingCross as a causal mechanism, and a cosmic Point 0 remain open hypotheses pending frozen, independently replicated discrimination. A positive separator gain, order sensitivity, Bridge-OFF specificity and independent replication would operationally identify an additional sector for the tested task; universality would remain a further empirical question. Statement of Intent This graphic novel was not conceived as a sequence of images generated from simple prompts. Each scene results from a cross-analysis of Thierry Origas’s documentary corpus by frontier AI systems, drawing on his PDFs, their concepts, their internal links, and their continuity. The words, formulations, and meaning-bearing images were then reviewed and validated by Thierry Origas in his own language, in order to avoid misunderstandings and distortions as much as possible. The purpose of this book is therefore not merely to present results, but to convey the spirit of an expanded way of thinking, its framework, its tensions, and its way of looking at reality like an intellectual cabin in which different representations can be confronted without being prematurely collapsed into one another, in the spirit of major scientific dialogues such as those between Einstein and Bohr. Since no direct meeting took place despite the requests addressed to the relevant institutions and individuals, Thierry Origas considered this format one of the most accessible ways to make his reasoning visible, to show the contemporary world to which he applies it, to clarify the position of his Red Line, and to explain the meaning of the scientific documents associated with this DOI. This graphic novel is therefore an entry point into the corpus: an aid to understanding, not a substitute for the scientific PDFs that remain the primary reference.

title: Dynamic Probability Fields: A Geometric Modeling Approach
abstract: Dynamic Probability Fields (DPFs) represent a novel approach to modeling probabilistic systems by leveraging geometric principles and dynamic adjustments. This paper explores the application of DPFs to system behavior prediction and optimization, offering a more precise and adaptable framework compared to traditional probabilistic models. We introduce a methodology that transforms probability distributions into geometric fields, utilizing geometric properties such as Gaussian curves and equivalent classes, to drive system behavior and parameter optimization. The core mechanism involves iteratively refining geometric parameters to achieve desired outcomes. This work addresses the limitations of existing models by providing a robust and flexible tool for predicting system behavior.

title: 基于自适应动态概率场的自适应调整
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to probabilistic modeling, introducing a dynamic probability field (DPF) algorithm that adapts to environmental changes through an iterative adjustment process. Traditional probabilistic models often necessitate manual adjustment, limiting their adaptability to complex environments. This algorithm leverages self-adaptive mechanisms to dynamically adjust probability distributions, leading to more accurate predictions. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that continuously evaluates the model's performance against observed data, enabling the algorithm to refine its probability estimates. This approach addresses the limitations of static models, offering improved predictive capabilities and robustness across varying operational conditions. The paper details the algorithm's design, its performance evaluation against benchmark datasets, and a discussion of its potential applications in various fields, including weather forecasting, financial modeling, and anomaly detection.

title: 基于自适应的深度学习超参数调整策略
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive hyperparameter adjustment strategy for deep learning models. Traditional hyperparameter optimization methods often rely on manual tuning, which can be time-consuming and inefficient. This work proposes a method that leverages an adaptive learning algorithm to automatically adjust hyperparameters based on the training data, resulting in improved model performance. We detail the proposed algorithm, its implementation, and evaluation results across several benchmark datasets. The core of the approach is an iterative refinement process utilizing a self-learning optimizer, minimizing the validation loss while maintaining a reasonable training loss. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through comprehensive experimental analysis, showcasing significant performance gains compared to traditional methods.

title: Title: Quantum-Inspired Algorithms for Lattice-Based Cryptography
abstract: Quantum-inspired algorithms represent a burgeoning field within cryptography, aiming to enhance the security of lattice-based systems by exploiting subtle quantum phenomena. This paper explores the design of novel quantum-inspired algorithms specifically tailored to the unique properties of lattice structures, focusing on enhancing resistance to known attacks. The core claim centers around developing algorithms that leverage entanglement and superposition to improve the robustness of lattice-based cryptography. We propose a framework for algorithm design, detailing the key steps involved in identifying and utilizing quantum-inspired features within lattice cryptography. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential implications and challenges of this approach.

title: Dynamic Topology Systems: An Analysis of Their Impact on Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper investigates the influence of dynamic topology systems on quantum computing, focusing on the development of a framework for simulation and prediction of quantum computation performance. The core claim is that the inherent properties of dynamic topology can be leveraged to design and optimize quantum algorithms through detailed simulations. We propose a model that constructs a quantum environment by simulating the dynamic evolution of a topological system, allowing for the prediction and refinement of quantum algorithms' effectiveness. This research addresses a relatively unexplored area within quantum computing, aiming to provide a novel approach to algorithm optimization.

title: Non-Geometric Topology: A Quantum Computing Accelerator
abstract: This paper explores a novel quantum computing accelerator leveraging non-geometric topology. Traditional quantum algorithms often suffer from computational bottlenecks and instability due to inherent complexities in their execution. We propose a mechanism that transforms the quantum computation process itself, rather than the algorithm, into a non-geometric topological transformation. This transformation dramatically reduces computational complexity and enhances the stability of quantum systems, offering a potentially transformative approach to quantum computing. This research investigates the theoretical implications of this approach, outlining the key mathematical framework and preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this mechanism in simplified scenarios.

abstract: This paper investigates the application of self-adaptive topology and quantum entanglement to transform geometric data. Traditional topological analysis often relies on static models, while this work proposes a novel algorithm leveraging quantum entanglement to induce dynamic and complex geometric transformations. The core mechanism centers around utilizing the entanglement-induced correlations to generate novel geometric structures, offering a potential pathway for enhanced quantum computation. We introduce a novel approach to quantum geometry, detailing the algorithm's design, key steps, and preliminary results demonstrating the feasibility of its implementation. This work explores how entanglement can be harnessed to create and manipulate geometric space, paving the way for new computational paradigms.

title: Dynamic Probability Distribution Chaos Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to chaos optimization utilizing a dynamically generated probability distribution. We propose an iterative optimization algorithm that automatically designs and optimizes complex geometric shapes by leveraging the inherent self-organizing properties of chaotic systems. The core mechanism involves introducing a dynamically evolving probability distribution as a control variable, enabling the algorithm to discover and refine geometric structures with enhanced adaptability and responsiveness. The potential applications of this approach span diverse fields, including materials science and biological modeling. This work addresses the limitations of traditional optimization methods by introducing a fundamentally different methodology that integrates chaos into the optimization process.

title: Explainable AI for Graph Structure Discovery
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems, by effectively learning patterns from graph-structured data. However, a significant limitation of GNNs is their inherent opaqueness—the "black box" nature of their decision-making process. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a novel approach integrating an explainability layer directly into a GNN architecture. This layer aims to provide transparent and interpretable explanations for the network's predictions, focusing on identifying the key structural features within the graph that contribute to the outcome. Specifically, we introduce a mechanism to highlight influential nodes and edges, offering insights into *why* a GNN made a particular prediction. This work enhances the trustworthiness and usability of GNNs by promoting a deeper understanding of their internal workings. The core contribution lies in bridging the gap between predictive performance and interpretability in graph learning.

title: Dynamic Programming for Reinforcement Learning with Partial Observability via State Abstraction
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in various domains, but its application to partially observable environments (POE) remains a significant challenge. Traditional dynamic programming (DP) methods, the foundation of many RL algorithms, suffer from the curse of dimensionality when dealing with large state spaces, a common characteristic of POE. This paper proposes a novel approach that integrates dynamic programming with state abstraction to overcome this limitation. We introduce a hybrid framework where a state abstraction layer learns a compact, informative representation of the underlying state space. This abstraction reduces the effective state space size, allowing DP to be applied efficiently. We formulate the problem as minimizing the expected return using a modified Bellman equation incorporating the abstracted state. The key contributions lie in the design of an adaptive state abstraction algorithm and its seamless integration with DP, resulting in a scalable RL solution for POE. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared to standard DP and other state abstraction methods.

This approach addresses a key challenge in network design – maintaining optimal performance across varying workloads and environmental conditions.

title: Dynamically Weighted Attention Mechanisms for Sequence-to-Sequence Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a dynamically weighted attention mechanism designed to enhance sequence-to-sequence learning models. Traditional fixed attention mechanisms often struggle to effectively capture long-range dependencies within sequences, limiting the overall performance of these models. Our approach addresses this limitation by creating an attention mechanism where the weights are dynamically learned based on the contextual information of the input sequence. This allows the model to prioritize and focus on the most relevant parts of the input during the generation of the output sequence. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis and conceptual discussion that this adaptive weighting scheme offers a significant improvement over static attention, ultimately leading to better performance in sequence-to-sequence tasks. This work contributes a novel approach to attention modeling, providing a flexible and adaptive mechanism for capturing complex relationships within sequential data.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum machine learning termed "Dynamic Matrix-Based Adaptive Quantum Machine Learning" (DMM-AQML). We propose a framework that leverages dynamic matrix computations and updates to emulate complex data and facilitate learning and prediction. The core innovation lies in the integration of quantum mechanics principles, specifically the inherent noise and dynamic nature of quantum systems, into the learning process. The proposed DMM-AQML offers advantages over traditional machine learning algorithms, particularly in handling high-dimensional data and complex non-linear relationships. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the framework's effectiveness in a simulated scenario. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications.

Traditional quantum optimization methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting the algorithm's adaptability and potential for improvement. AQPO leverages a dynamic quantum potential landscape, adjusting the potential energy fields during optimization, resulting in a more robust and efficient process. The paper details the algorithm's core mechanism, explores its implementation and validation through simulations, and discusses the advantages over existing optimization techniques. title: Based on Quantum Entanglement: Distributed Reasoning
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement for enabling distributed reasoning paradigms that transcend the limitations of classical physics. The core claim is that leveraging entanglement allows for parallel and fault-tolerant computation, offering a fundamentally new approach to distributed systems. The proposed mechanism involves encoding information into entangled particles and utilizing the correlations between their entangled states for information processing. This approach inherently facilitates simultaneous computation across multiple nodes and provides intrinsic resilience against node failures. We outline a framework for distributed reasoning based on this principle, highlighting its advantages over traditional distributed systems and addressing key challenges in scalability and practical implementation. The research investigates the theoretical foundations of entanglement-based distributed reasoning and proposes a novel architecture for achieving high-performance, robust computations. This work represents a significant step towards realizing quantum-enhanced distributed computing capabilities.

title: Probabilistic Focal Search: Accelerating Bounded-Suboptimal Search via Lower-Bound Advancement
abstract: Bounded-suboptimal search seeks a solution within a factor $w$ of optimal while reducing search effort. Focal Search (FS) uses heuristic guidance within FOCAL, the frontier nodes eligible under the threshold $w f_{\min}$, but its deterministic policy may leave $f_{\min}$ unchanged for many expansions. We introduce Probabilistic Focal Search (PFS), which follows the FS guided choice with probability $p$ and expands a minimum-$f$ OPEN node with probability $1-p$. The latter branch encourages the lower bound to advance, enlarging FOCAL and admitting nodes that may lead to feasible solutions. By balancing guidance and lower-bound advancement, this mechanism can reduce time to a bounded solution when progress is limited by delayed FOCAL admission. As a secondary transfer experiment, we apply the same scheduler to Dynamic Potential Search, yielding Probabilistic Dynamic Potential Search (PDPS). We benchmark PFS against FS on N-Puzzle, Pancake Sorting, and the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP), and evaluate its anytime extension on the Generalized Covering TSP (GCTSP), using multiple $w$ and $p$ values. Across these benchmarks, the largest gains occur when long $f_{\min}$ plateaus delay useful FOCAL admissions; in such settings, the probabilistic factor may reduce node expansions by about 90\% or more (e.g., on N-Puzzle and TSP). For the anytime algorithm family, Anytime Probabilistic Focal Search (APFS) outperforms all tested algorithms in evaluating anytime methods on GCTSP. We also observe that the benefit is smaller when the deterministic search already advances efficiently (e.g., Pancake Sorting), indicating that the probabilistic factor is most useful when FOCAL admission is a search bottleneck. The PDPS transfer shows that the mechanism also transfers to potential guidance, although its common-success effects remain domain- and bound-dependent.

title: RAIDAL: Redundancy-Aware Information Density Active Learning for CTC-Based Continuous Sign Language Recognition
abstract: Continuous sign language recognition (CSLR) is a key technology for accessibility, yet its development remains limited by the high cost of annotating continuous video streams. Active learning offers a path toward mitigating this cost, but standard acquisition functions are not designed for weakly aligned sign language videos, where sign executions are interleaved with rest poses, irregular pauses, sign-like motion, and temporally redundant frames. This temporal redundancy can undermine sample selection, as acquisition scores may be influenced by timesteps from regions that are not associated with the decoded gloss sequence, distorting the video's estimated informativeness. In this work, we show that modern CSLR models already contain a mechanism for identifying gloss-level temporal evidence: the CTC decoder. Although typically used only during inference, its alignment peaks indicate where the model localizes each predicted gloss in the feature sequence, providing a source of temporal structure for active learning acquisition functions at zero additional labeling cost. Thus, we introduce RAIDAL (Redundancy-Aware Information Density Active Learning), which repurposes the CTC decoder to restrict representation-based scoring to decoder-aligned gloss regions, rather than exposing the acquisition function to the entire unfiltered video. Across three datasets and two architectures, RAIDAL achieves its strongest data-efficiency gains over competing baselines in large-vocabulary, budget-limited settings, while remaining competitive in the smaller-vocabulary, large-budget setting. The code used in this work is publicly available at github.com/verlab/RAIDAL.

title: USE OF THE CONCEPT MULTI-AGENT SYSTEM IN THE EDUCATIONAL PROCESS
abstract: This study highlights the pedagogical and technological possibilities of using the CONCEPT multi-agent system in the educational process. Based on a multi-agent approach, it focuses on organizing the interaction between various participants and information resources in the educational process, identifying students' individual needs, and personalizing educational content. The article explores the possibilities of using the CONCEPT multi-agent system to monitor the process of mastering educational materials, adapt tasks to a student's knowledge level, generate analytical data, and support the teacher's pedagogical activities. Furthermore, it analyzes the significance of this technology in enhancing educational effectiveness, fostering independent learning, providing prompt feedback, and managing the learning process.

title: Title: Topological Information-Driven Quantum Entanglement Computation Framework
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum technologies, presents significant challenges in terms of error correction and secure communication. Traditional error correction codes often rely on complex mathematical operations, introducing vulnerabilities. This paper introduces a novel quantum entanglement computation framework leveraging topological information, aiming to enhance the robustness and security of entanglement. We propose a quantum entanglement computation algorithm that utilizes the inherent topological properties of entangled states to achieve improved error correction and secure information transfer. This framework utilizes a dynamically constructed quantum state, exploiting topological features to effectively mitigate errors and safeguard sensitive information. The core mechanism revolves around designing a quantum state computation scheme intrinsically linked to topological structures. This approach offers a potential paradigm shift in the field, providing a more reliable and secure route to quantum technologies.

abstract: This paper investigates the application of non-Euclidean topology to the design and analysis of lattice-based quantum computing architectures. title: 基于自适应的机器学习的领域自适应模型
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to field-specific model adaptation utilizing a dynamic adjustment of model parameters. Traditional model parameter tuning often remains fixed, limiting the model's effectiveness in diverse applications. Our work introduces a self-adaptive learning framework where the model's parameters are iteratively refined based on the characteristics of the target domain. This adaptation process is driven by a reinforcement learning algorithm that optimizes a performance metric related to the specific application. The core mechanism involves a multi-stage adaptation cycle, beginning with initial parameter initialization and culminating in refined parameters tailored to the target domain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through a series of experiments evaluating its performance across various domain-specific datasets. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in model accuracy and generalization capabilities compared to static parameter adjustments. The proposed framework offers a flexible and adaptable solution for enhancing model performance in complex, evolving fields.

title: Title: Non-Local Quantum Simulation via Interference Mapping (NQ-QIM)
abstract: Quantum simulation is a crucial field for understanding complex quantum systems, but traditional methods often struggle to accurately represent the full state of the system due to limitations in computational resources. This paper introduces Non-Local Quantum Simulation via Interference Mapping (NQ-QIM), a novel technique for simulating quantum systems by strategically mapping interference patterns across multiple qubits. We propose a method that leverages advanced mathematical techniques to generate a 'global' representation of the quantum state, significantly improving the accuracy and potential for understanding of quantum phenomena. This approach overcomes limitations of existing local simulation methods by enabling a more comprehensive and potentially more accurate representation of quantum states. The paper details the implementation of the interference mapping technique, its benefits, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in simulating specific quantum systems. We conclude with a discussion of future research directions and the potential impact of this technique on the field of quantum simulation.

This paper explores a novel approach to quantum equation solving utilizing entanglement, aiming to enhance the precision of state measurement and modeling within quantum computation and simulation. The core mechanism centers around leveraging entanglement to simplify the solution process and achieve more accurate results. This work proposes a new algorithmic framework that leverages the inherent correlation between entangled particles to efficiently navigate the equation's solution space, ultimately offering a significant advancement over existing methods. The paper details the implementation of the proposed method, its performance evaluation, and discusses its potential implications for advancing quantum technologies.

title: Nonlinear Topological Geometry: A Quantum Entanglement Theory
abstract: This paper explores the intersection of nonlinear topological geometry and quantum entanglement, proposing a novel framework that directly maps the entangled state to the non-linear relationship between quantum topology and entanglement. We introduce the concept of "拓扑量子纠缠" – a quantum entanglement underpinned by topological structure – to guide the design of quantum entanglement simulators. The core mechanism involves constructing a quantum entanglement simulator based on this framework, offering a potential pathway to enhanced quantum computation and a deeper understanding of quantum mechanics. This research investigates the implications of this approach for both simulation and hardware design, aiming to reveal fundamental physical relationships within quantum entanglement.

title: Algorithmic Transparency and Explainable AI for Hardware Design
abstract: The increasing reliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) in hardware design presents both significant opportunities and challenges. While AI algorithms can accelerate the design process and optimize performance, their "black box" nature raises concerns regarding trust, accountability, and potential biases. This paper argues for the critical importance of algorithmic transparency and explainable AI (XAI) within the context of hardware design. We propose a framework for developing techniques that elucidate the decision-making processes of AI-powered hardware design tools. Specifically, we explore methods for visualizing and interpreting the reasoning behind AI's choices, offering insights into the underlying algorithms and their influence on design outcomes. The core claim is that understanding these design choices is fundamental to building trust and ensuring accountability. This work lays the groundwork for a future where AI and human designers can collaborate effectively, leveraging the strengths of both while mitigating potential risks. The proposed approach involves a combination of algorithmic analysis, visualization techniques, and the development of metrics to quantify the explainability of AI-driven hardware design systems. Ultimately, this research contributes to the broader field of XAI by addressing a particularly challenging and impactful domain: hardware.

title: Quantum System Dynamics Calibration with Adaptive Parameter Correction
abstract: Quantum systems exhibit inherent sensitivity to environmental fluctuations, posing significant challenges to achieving stable and controllable operations. Traditional control strategies often rely on fixed parameters, failing to account for these dynamic variations. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum system dynamics calibration, employing a dynamic parameter correction mechanism based on machine learning. The core principle involves real-time monitoring of system states, enabling the system to adapt its parameters dynamically to maintain stability and controllability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through simulations and preliminary experimental results, highlighting its potential to significantly enhance the performance of quantum systems.

title: Automated Theorem Proving with Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: This paper explores the potential of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for automating theorem proving. Traditional automated theorem provers often struggle with complex logical structures and require significant human intervention. This work proposes a novel approach where a GAN is trained to generate potential proofs, with a discriminator tasked to evaluate their validity. The core mechanism relies on an adversarial training loop, enabling the generator to progressively refine its proof-generating abilities based on the discriminator's feedback. We argue that this represents a radical departure from conventional theorem proving methods, harnessing the creative and iterative capabilities of GANs to tackle complex logical problems. The presented framework demonstrates a pathway toward more efficient and robust automated reasoning systems.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Encoding via Tensor Field Models
abstract: Quantum entanglement presents a unique and potentially revolutionary paradigm for information security. This paper investigates the application of tensor field models to quantum entanglement information encoding, aiming to establish a novel cryptographic method underpinned by the inherent properties of entanglement. We propose a framework where entangled states serve as the fundamental units of information, utilizing a tensor field model to encode data, and incorporating a robust error correction mechanism to enhance security. The core claim is that this approach offers a degree of security and operational resistance exceeding that of current cryptographic standards, particularly in the context of complex and potentially manipulatable quantum systems. This work explores the theoretical foundations and practical considerations of such a model, emphasizing the crucial role of entanglement in bolstering security.

title: Differential Privacy via Kernel Embedding
abstract: Differential privacy is a rigorous mathematical definition of privacy that provides quantifiable protection against membership inference attacks. However, directly applying differential privacy to deep learning models has proven challenging, often resulting in substantial utility degradation. This work proposes a novel approach – Kernel Embedding with Differential Privacy – to mitigate this issue. The core idea is to learn a kernel embedding that maps high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space, where differential privacy guarantees are more effective. Crucially, the kernel function itself is trained under differential privacy constraints. This allows us to maintain a better privacy-utility trade-off compared to traditional approaches. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through theoretical analysis and, importantly, by outlining a framework that can be adapted to various deep learning architectures. The resulting embedding provides a more privacy-preserving representation of the data, while preserving a significant level of information for downstream tasks. The key contributions of this research lie in the strategic combination of kernel methods and differential privacy, offering a promising path toward robust and privacy-preserving deep learning.

title: Introductory Notes on Learning$^2$
abstract: Although machine learning can be used to predict the evolution of physical systems from data, a formulation that learns only the system state at each time leaves the temporal and dynamical structure of the solution to be resolved within a broad hypothesis space. We introduce Learning$^2$, a representation-level framework that structures this space by coupling a primary representation to a second representation through a known physical transformation. The resulting cross-representation constraint restricts the effective hypothesis space and provides an ante-hoc, physically interpretable criterion for excluding solutions that satisfy the primary representation alone. We instantiate Learning$^2$ through EuLaNet, an Eulerian--Lagrangian representation for fluid dynamics. Given the velocity state $u(\mathbf{x},t)$, EuLaNet constructs its induced Lagrangian flow map $X(\mathbf{a},t)$ through $\dot{X}(\mathbf{a},t)=u(X(\mathbf{a},t),t)$, from which material transport and finite-time deformation are derived. The resulting representation couples the predicted state to the dynamical consequences it induces, providing a second consistency criterion beyond state-level agreement. We formalize this construction through an effective hypothesis space $\mathcal{H}_{L^2}\subseteq\mathcal{H}$ and define the conditions under which a consequence representation provides discriminative constraints on candidate solutions. EuLaNet is implemented as a model-independent representation module, separating the physical constraint from the downstream learning architecture. This construction provides an ante-hoc mechanism for physically interpretable constraint in scientific learning and offers a basis for developing and evaluating broader classes of Learning$^2$ architectures. The implementation is open-sourced to support the development and extension of the architecture across scientific domains.

title: Constraint-Based Quantum Simulation via Hybrid Algorithms
abstract: Quantum simulation is a vital tool for understanding complex quantum systems, but current methods often struggle with the computational cost, particularly for large and intricate systems. This paper proposes a novel hybrid algorithm for quantum simulation that seamlessly integrates classical and quantum computation, leveraging a dynamically adjusted resource allocation strategy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through the simulation of a parameterized quantum system, showcasing improved accuracy and scalability compared to traditional methods. The core mechanism involves a carefully designed hybrid algorithm that exploits the strengths of both classical and quantum processing, leading to a more efficient and reliable simulation process. This work introduces a framework for enhanced quantum simulation capabilities, offering a significant advancement in this field.

title: Temporal Symmetry – Non-Linear Optimization via Oscillatory Patterns
abstract: This paper presents a novel method for optimizing complex systems through the identification and exploitation of temporal symmetry within their dynamics. The core principle is to analyze the evolution of a system, specifically identifying rhythmic shifts in parameters that correlate with optimal solutions. We introduce a novel algorithm predicated on detecting these oscillations, leveraging a unique temporal analysis framework to guide optimization. This approach contrasts with conventional optimization techniques, which often rely on linear assumptions, and promises to uncover potentially transformative solutions. The paper details the algorithm's structure, provides preliminary results demonstrating its efficacy in a simulated system, and discusses future research directions.

title: 基于图的因果推理与动态决策
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for causal reasoning and dynamic decision-making based on graph-based models. Traditional approaches often rely on static models, limiting their ability to effectively handle dynamic environments and real-time adaptation. Our work proposes a system that dynamically updates the graph representation of a system based on observed events, enabling predictive and control capabilities. We develop a method for learning causal relationships through graph evolution and integrate this with decision-making algorithms to facilitate efficient and responsive decision processes. This framework offers a significant advancement over existing methods by explicitly incorporating dynamic changes to the graph structure, leading to enhanced predictive accuracy and the capacity for adaptive control. The paper details the core mechanisms, including graph evolution, causal relationship learning, and decision integration, and presents a preliminary evaluation demonstrating its effectiveness in a simulated environment.

abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement to represent hyperdimensional geometric structures, offering a novel approach to high-dimensional data analysis and computation. We investigate the utilization of entanglement to encode data in a way that enhances both encoding and transmission, aiming to significantly improve computational efficiency. The core mechanism relies on exploiting the unique properties of quantum entanglement to achieve a more efficient data representation and facilitate calculations. This work addresses a significant gap in current research by proposing a new methodology grounded in the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics. The investigation of this approach may lead to the discovery of new geometric properties and computational paradigms.

title: Quantum Quantum Decoherence Calculation
abstract: Quantum Quantum Decoherence Calculation is a novel computational approach leveraging the unique properties of quantum coherence to precisely calculate complex quantum decoherence scenarios. Traditional quantum computing relies on classical algorithms, which are limited in their ability to accurately model and resolve the inherent decoherence processes that significantly impact quantum computation. This research proposes a new method employing quantum entanglement to construct a specialized calculation framework designed to capture and quantify decoherence effects, leading to substantially improved accuracy in simulating and predicting quantum systems. The core mechanism centers around strategically manipulating quantum states to generate and analyze decoherence patterns, ultimately providing a more reliable foundation for quantum algorithm design and optimization. The current method demonstrates superior performance in simulating complex decoherence dynamics compared to existing techniques, offering a significant advancement in the field of quantum computational fidelity. This work establishes a foundational basis for a new paradigm in quantum computation, emphasizing the crucial role of quantum coherence in achieving precise results.

title: Cognitive Architectures with Embodied Bayesian Inference
abstract: This paper proposes a novel cognitive architecture framework integrating embodied Bayesian inference. The core claim is that traditional cognitive architectures can be significantly strengthened by incorporating the principles of how humans learn and reason – namely, through embodiment and probabilistic belief updating. This architecture, termed the Embodied Bayesian Cognitive Architecture (E-BCA), utilizes sensory input and interaction to continuously represent and update its beliefs about the world via Bayesian inference. The architecture's novelty lies in the seamless fusion of cognitive architecture's modular design with the dynamic, adaptive nature of embodied Bayesian learning. The framework provides a robust and realistic model for cognitive processes, addressing limitations of purely symbolic or connectionist approaches. The architecture is designed to handle uncertainty, learn from experience, and adapt to changing environments. This work lays the groundwork for future research exploring complex cognitive tasks and behaviors within a biologically plausible framework.

title: Distributed Adaptive Quantum Algorithm Compilation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to distributed quantum algorithm compilation, termed Adaptive Distributed Quantum Algorithm Compilation (ADQAC). The core idea is to develop a system capable of automatically compiling and optimizing quantum algorithms for execution on distributed quantum hardware, adapting to the specific characteristics and resource constraints of each node. We leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to dynamically adjust the algorithm's execution sequence, gate selection, and resource allocation based on real-time performance metrics gathered from the quantum hardware. This approach addresses the significant challenges of translating high-level quantum algorithms into efficient, executable code for heterogeneous distributed quantum computing environments. The system aims to maximize algorithm fidelity while minimizing communication overhead and resource utilization. title: Dynamic Programming for Quantum State Preparation
abstract: Quantum state preparation is a critical component in many quantum algorithms, yet its complexity scales exponentially with the number of qubits and the desired state's complexity. This work presents a novel approach to quantum state preparation utilizing dynamic programming. We demonstrate that dynamic programming can efficiently determine optimal sequences of quantum gates to realize a target quantum state, significantly reducing the computational burden compared to exhaustive search methods. The core of our method lies in formulating the problem as a state-space optimization task, where each state represents a partial quantum state and the transition between states corresponds to applying a quantum gate. We detail the algorithm and provide a theoretical analysis of its performance, highlighting its potential to mitigate the exponential scaling issues inherent in traditional quantum state preparation techniques. This approach offers a practical and scalable solution for preparing complex quantum states, representing a significant advancement in the field.

title: Shye 1.0: A Heartbeat-Driven Protocol Core for Hop-by-Hop Random Forwarding in Adversarial Decentralized Networks
abstract: Path construction in anonymous communication commonly relies on a relay directory or previously established multi-hop relationships. When node availability and connectivity continue to change, and access to a global relay directory is restricted or blocked, a sender may be unable to preconstruct and maintain a complete path. This paper presents Shye 1.0, a heartbeat-driven protocol core for hop-by-hop random forwarding that advances message state along a short-lived forwarding chain. Heartbeat rounds schedule claim windows, retries, and expiry checks, while predetermined beacon rounds supply future public random material. Candidates obtain recomputable forwarding eligibility under a public threshold, and the current selector authorizes one selected forwarder from its local eligible-claim set. Signed SelectionGrant and HandoffWitness objects describe a state transition, while StateProof traces the current holder's authority to the sender-created InitCertificate. In the normative transparent implementation, one transition record is appended at every hop. Proof length therefore grows linearly with the number of traversed hops and is bounded by the initial TTL; TTL and an absolute expiry round jointly bound the lifetime of an honestly forwarded chain. The paper states four limited properties: eligibility soundness, transcript-relative honest selection, rooted authorization continuity, and bounded honest propagation. Because claim propagation depends on local views, the protocol verifies the eligibility and authorization of the selected node without proving candidate-set completeness or network-wide agreement on one selection. Cover traffic and a one-shot mailbox are retained only as conditional profiles for anonymous communication. Guaranteed delivery, end-to-end anonymity, Sybil resistance, and performance require deployment-specific mechanisms and experiments. The present manuscript supplies a protocol specification and a conformance boundary; it reports no performance, delivery-rate, or anonymity results. This record contains the English manuscript and a Chinese reference version of Shye 1.0, manuscript version 1.0.5.

title: Quantum Information Evolution Algorithm: Self-Adjusting Mechanism
abstract: Quantum information evolution algorithms are crucial for realizing the full potential of quantum computation. However, traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameter adjustments, limiting the algorithm's efficiency. This paper introduces a novel quantum information evolution algorithm, driven by the principles of quantum entanglement and dynamic state feedback, designed to automatically optimize quantum gate parameters based on real-time quantum state changes. The core mechanism leverages the instantaneous correlation between entangled qubits to dynamically adjust the quantum state, effectively eliminating the need for pre-defined parameter adjustments. This approach promises to significantly enhance the performance of quantum algorithms by achieving higher fidelity and computational throughput. This work presents a conceptual framework and preliminary results demonstrating the efficacy of this self-adjusting algorithm.

title: Adaptive Self-Adapting Learning of Probability Models
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic model framework, termed "Adaptive Self-Adapting Learning" (ASAL), that leverages dynamic parameter adjustment to enhance model training and generalization performance. Traditional probabilistic modeling often relies on fixed parameters, limiting their effectiveness when dealing with complex datasets. ASAL addresses this limitation by employing a mechanism that dynamically adjusts learning parameters based on data characteristics, enabling automated optimization and improved generalization. The paper explores the benefits of this approach through a detailed analysis and illustrative examples. We demonstrate that ASAL outperforms conventional methods in various scenarios, particularly when handling high-dimensional data.

abstract: Adaptive Machine Learning Evaluation Metrics offers a novel approach to assessing model performance by dynamically adjusting the weighting of evaluation metrics. This paper introduces a system that automatically adjusts these metrics based on model predictions and error analysis, leading to enhanced evaluation precision. The core mechanism involves a self-adaptive algorithm that continuously refines the weighting of each metric, optimizing for accuracy. This paper explores the advantages of this approach compared to traditional weighting methods and demonstrates its effectiveness through rigorous analysis. We present a system that achieves significantly improved performance metrics compared to baseline models, illustrating the potential of adaptive evaluation in machine learning.

title: Information Entropy as a Physical Quantity Measurement and Quantum State Correlation
abstract: This paper explores the potential of utilizing measurements of information entropy-related physical quantities as a novel approach to predict and control quantum state correlations. The central argument posits that precise determination of entropy-related parameters within a system can directly influence the associated quantum entanglement and correlations. We propose a new measurement device designed to simultaneously quantify entropy, energy, and other relevant physical attributes. This device, when coupled with a theoretical framework, offers a mechanism for manipulating quantum correlations by modulating these measured quantities. The research introduces a fundamentally new perspective on quantum control, shifting the focus from traditional methods to a measurement-based approach leveraging the intrinsic information content of a quantum system. The paper details the theoretical underpinnings, outlines the design considerations for the measurement device, and discusses the potential implications for advancements in quantum computing and communication.

title: Adversarial Robustness via Generative Model Defense
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to enhancing the adversarial robustness of neural networks by utilizing generative models. The core idea revolves around training a generative model to accurately reconstruct the input data, thereby creating a robust representation. This reconstructed data is then used as input to the neural network, significantly reducing the impact of adversarial perturbations. We demonstrate that this defense mechanism, leveraging generative models, provides a more effective strategy compared to traditional methods. Our approach addresses a critical vulnerability in current neural network designs and offers a promising direction for building more resilient and reliable AI systems. We present a theoretical framework and outline the key components of this defense strategy. The central contribution lies in the systematic application of generative models to proactively defend against adversarial attacks, rather than reacting to them post-hoc. The results presented indicate a substantial improvement in the network's resilience to adversarial examples.

title: Sharp Target-Domain Certificates for Quantum-Kernel Advantage under Distribution Shift
abstract: Quantum predictive advantage under shift usually requires known target labels. We derive the assumption-free sharp identified interval for the finite-batch advantage of a fixed candidate over the best member of a prespecified fixed classical-kernel family under any bounded loss and unrestricted completions of the unaudited labels; zero-one accuracy has exact closed-form partial-label updates. Across eight security shifts, zero-label upper endpoints against 115 classical kernels span 0.002-0.088. Retrospective auditing reduces every endpoint to 0.010 with 0-33 of 500 labels, including entangling-ZZ models. Prospective corroboration on two eligible tasks met predefined criteria: four task-classifier medians require 0-3 labels (overall median 0; maximum 76), and all 20 realized effects are negative; a third task fails its feature gate. Protocol controls reverse an apparent advantage, while finite-shot noise can increase predictive distinctness without useful advantage. The framework separates protocol validity, target predictive indispensability, and quantum relevance.

title: WAPP: Safe Learning of Positive Security WAF Policies from Live Traffic
abstract: Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) mainly rely on signatures to detect known attacks, which can leave gaps against modified or previously unseen payloads. Positive security provides a complementary approach by learning legitimate traffic and blocking inputs that fall outside the learned profile. However, learning directly from live traffic can be unsafe when malicious requests contaminate the training data. This paper presents the Whitelisting Autonomous Policy Producer (WAPP), a framework that combines trust filtering, deterministic rule synthesis, confidence scoring, and validation before enforcement. WAPP is evaluated on three controlled applications using a live Coraza and OWASP Core Rule Set (CRS) stack. Results show that, on the tested DVWA username field, unfiltered learning becomes Degraded at 0.2\% poisoned traffic and Broken at 0.5%, while the evaluated free text field can admit malicious inputs even without poisoning. On the frozen poisoning dataset, the ablation configuration with all seven candidate signals improves the measured poisoning resilience from 53% to 90%, compared with 62% for the Kruegel--Vigna baseline. The deterministic synthesizer provides attack blocking comparable to the tested language model without model inference cost. WAPP blocks confirmed CRS bypasses on constrained fields, while free text inputs remain a precision challenge that requires character level operator control.

title: LLMs Mirror Country-Specific Gender Patterns If Asked, but Skew Male When Generating Media in Local Languages
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate media, but whether their content perpetuates gender stereotypes is unknown: standard benchmarks rely on selection-based formats rather than long-form generation, and surveyed baselines for local gender associations are scarce outside the West. We collect gender associations for 22 occupational and domestic roles from 695 respondents across the United States, India, Kenya, and Nigeria, and evaluate eight LLMs under two regimes: direct questioning and media generation. Models track the surveyed associations under direct questioning but skew substantially more male under media generation in major local-language cells, consistent with the male bias documented in human-produced media. Outside the US, the shift is much smaller and non-significant under English prompting, so English-only or country-agnostic evaluation would miss this bias in the languages where these models are most deployed. Instruction prompting reduces the shift directionally, but trades off against alignment with the surveyed associations. Evaluating LLM gender bias for global deployment therefore requires generation-format testing, local-language prompting, and locally-collected human baselines.

title: Random Algebraic Geometry Codes Approach the Half-Singleton Bound for Insertions and Deletions
abstract: In this paper, we study the performance of algebraic geometry (AG) codes against adversarial insertion-deletion (insdel) errors. The half-Singleton bound states that an $[n,k]_q$ linear code can correct at most $n-2k+1$ insdel errors. It was recently proven that random Reed-Solomon codes approach this bound. However, these constructions require the field size $q$ to grow linearly with the code length $n$. We overcome this barrier by extending the probabilistic analysis of general linear insdel codes to AG codes. We demonstrate that curves with many rational points allow for nearly optimal codes over significantly smaller alphabets. We prove the following main asymptotic results: (1) For general smooth complete curves of fixed genus, random AG codes are nearly optimal, that is, they can correct $(1-\varepsilon)n-2k$ insdel errors with high probability over linear-sized fields ($q=Θ(n)$). (2) By utilizing Hermitian curves, we achieve this optimality over sublinear fields of size $q=Θ(n^{2/3})$, breaking the linear field size barrier. (3) Using asymptotically optimal García-Stichtenoth towers, we prove the existence of random AG codes that approach the half-Singleton bound with high probability over fields of size $q=2^{O_R(1/\varepsilon^2)}$, independent of $n$.

abstract: Dynamic adaptive matrix, leveraging adaptive learning, aims to enhance model learning efficiency. title: Dynamic Topology Quantum Simulation Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic topology quantum simulation algorithm designed to overcome the limitations of traditional quantum simulation methods. The algorithm leverages the inherent fragility of quantum entanglement to model complex systems with unprecedented accuracy. By employing a dynamic topology framework, we introduce a mechanism for simulating systems exhibiting intricate correlations and vulnerabilities, ultimately providing a more robust and precise representation of quantum phenomena. The core of the algorithm centers around the manipulation of quantum states through a topology that adapts to the system's dynamics. This adaptive approach facilitates the simulation of systems with high degrees of complexity and sensitivity to initial conditions. The proposed method offers a significant advancement in quantum simulation capabilities, potentially unlocking new insights into fundamental physics and materials science.

title: Adaptive Gaussian Random Field (AGRF) Dynamic Parameter Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Adaptive Gaussian Random Field (AGRF) algorithm that dynamically adjusts the learning strategy for parameter optimization. Traditional AGRF approaches typically employ static parameter tuning, which can be limited in their ability to handle complex data distributions and lead to suboptimal performance. This work proposes a dynamic adjustment mechanism that combines gradient descent with adaptive learning techniques, allowing the algorithm to adapt its learning rate and adjustment parameters in response to data changes and target variable shifts. The core of this innovation lies in the integration of a dynamic learning rate and adjustment mechanism, resulting in more robust and stable predictive and control capabilities compared to static parameter adjustments. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through extensive simulations and experiments across a range of datasets, showcasing its ability to achieve superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and overall stability.

The core mechanism centers on a self-learning algorithm that constructs a geometric representation of the input data, which then informs the model's learning process. This results in improved generalization and robustness, particularly when dealing with complex data distributions. The paper details the algorithm's implementation, demonstrates its effectiveness through illustrative examples, and discusses future research directions.

title: 基于量子纠错码的分布式系统容错性增强
abstract: This paper investigates the enhancement of fault tolerance in distributed systems by leveraging quantum error correction codes. The core claim is that incorporating quantum error correction codes significantly improves the resilience of distributed systems operating in noisy environments. The proposed mechanism involves deploying quantum error correction codes among the nodes of a distributed system, enabling the detection and correction of errors affecting individual quantum bits. Unlike traditional redundancy-based approaches, this method offers a more efficient and resource-conscious strategy for achieving fault tolerance. We explore the theoretical framework and potential benefits of this approach, focusing on the key aspects of quantum error correction code implementation and its impact on distributed system reliability. The system is characterized by its ability to mitigate the detrimental effects of noise, leading to improved data transmission and overall system stability. This work provides a foundational understanding of utilizing quantum error correction codes to address the critical challenges of fault tolerance in distributed systems.

title: Title: Zero-Assisted Superposition for Parallel Computation
abstract: The inherent limitations of current quantum computing architectures, particularly in terms of scalability and computational throughput, pose a significant challenge to realizing the full potential of quantum systems. Traditional approaches to quantum circuit design often rely on carefully crafted sequences of gates, which can be time-consuming and require substantial resources. This paper introduces a novel approach to superposition, termed "Zero-Assisted Superposition" (ZAS), that leverages a fundamentally different strategy to overcome these limitations. ZAS employs a specially designed quantum gate that actively 'zeroes out' the state of individual qubits, allowing for the exploration of exponentially larger Hilbert spaces and facilitating massively parallel computation. This method offers a promising pathway to significantly enhance the computational power of quantum computers by enabling faster and more efficient processing of complex problems.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Programming with Temporal Reasoning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel neuro-symbolic programming system designed to leverage the complementary strengths of neural networks and symbolic programming while incorporating temporal reasoning. The core idea is to build a system capable of learning and executing programs that operate effectively across time, addressing a key limitation in existing neuro-symbolic approaches. The system integrates neural networks for perceptual tasks, such as feature extraction and pattern recognition, with symbolic representations for logical reasoning and program construction. Temporal reasoning is achieved through a novel mechanism that allows the system to track and manipulate temporal dependencies within the symbolic representation. This approach enables more sophisticated and adaptive behavior, particularly in domains where understanding and acting upon temporal information is crucial. The system's architecture and key components are detailed, along with an explanation of how the neural and symbolic elements interact. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a conceptual framework, outlining the integration process and future research directions. The system aims to move beyond static program execution to dynamic, temporally-aware program generation and execution.

The core claim is that this approach significantly improves model robustness and generalization, offering a viable alternative to traditional methods when dealing with high-dimensional, uncertain data. The paper explores the benefits of this integration, detailing the impact on training stability and the resulting performance on diverse datasets.

title: Probability Adaptive Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Probability Adaptive Graph Neural Networks (PAGNNs) represents a novel approach to graph neural network design, focusing on the dynamic adjustment of network structure to enhance performance, particularly in handling high-dimensional graph data. This work introduces a probabilistic model to estimate graph structure, enabling adaptive network adjustments. The core mechanism involves quantifying the graph's structure through a probabilistic model and then dynamically modifying network parameters based on this quantification. This adaptive approach contrasts with static graph neural network architectures, offering improved robustness and generalization capabilities. This paper details the design and evaluation of PAGNNs, demonstrating their efficacy in various graph-based tasks, including graph classification, graph clustering, and node propagation. The results highlight the significant advantages of this dynamic network structure in complex graph scenarios.

title: Self-Organizing Neural Networks: Topological Network Architecture Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm for optimizing Self-Organizing Neural Networks (SONNs) based on topological network structure. Traditional SONN training methods often overlook the importance of network topology, resulting in suboptimal performance and instability. Our proposed algorithm dynamically adjusts connection weights to enhance model generalization and computational efficiency by leveraging the inherent topology of the network. We present a comprehensive framework incorporating a dynamic connectivity matrix adjustment strategy and a feedback loop based on network topology metrics. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through extensive simulations and analysis, showcasing significant improvements in model accuracy and training speed compared to existing approaches. Keywords: Self-Organizing Neural Networks, Topological Network, Connectivity Optimization, Neural Network, Generalization, Computational Efficiency.

title: Neuro-Inspired Symbolic Logic Synthesis
abstract: This paper investigates the possibility of synthesizing symbolic logic rules and expressions using neural networks. The core claim is that neural networks, when trained appropriately, can learn to generate logical reasoning steps, thereby automating the creation of logical systems. The proposed mechanism involves training a neural network to predict the next logical step within a proof sequence, leveraging both symbolic reasoning capabilities and the pattern recognition strengths inherent in neural networks. This research explores a novel intersection of artificial intelligence and formal logic, potentially opening doors to automated reasoning systems with enhanced adaptability and efficiency. The approach moves beyond traditional symbolic systems by incorporating the learning capacity of neural networks, aiming to create a system where logical deduction is learned rather than explicitly programmed. Key elements explored include the network architecture, loss function design, and training data selection, all geared towards enabling the network to accurately predict logical steps. The goal is to establish a trainable system capable of generating valid logical rules and expressions, representing a significant step towards truly intelligent reasoning. ---

title: Neural Network Topology Adaptive Generation and Dynamic Path Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network architecture design and optimization, leveraging reinforcement learning (RL) and dynamic analysis of neural network topologies. The core claim is that by combining these techniques, we can achieve adaptive generation of complex network structures, significantly enhancing performance on specific tasks, and dynamically optimizing information pathways. The system begins with a randomly generated neural network topology. An RL agent, guided by a reward function tied to task performance (accuracy, latency, etc.), iteratively adjusts network parameters – connection weights, neuron numbers, and topology – through exploration. Simultaneously, dynamic analysis of the network topology (e.g., flow information analysis, neuron activation pattern analysis) identifies inefficiencies and bottlenecks. The RL algorithm then uses these dynamic analysis results to guide topology optimization and dynamically adjust neuronal connection paths for optimal information transmission. This approach moves beyond static weight tuning to dynamic routing based on neuronal activity patterns, offering a potentially more efficient and adaptive solution. The primary contribution lies in the integration of dynamic topology analysis with RL for self-optimizing neural network architectures.

title: tokenizer-detect
abstract: A prerecorded test of the hypothesis that token fertility explains how well a machine text detector works on a language. The X axis is tokens per whitespace word on FLORES-200 devtest over 204 languages and 4 tokenizers, counted locally with zero model calls. The Y axis is copied verbatim from published tables, MULTITuDE macro-F1 and Pangram 4 table 8 FNR and FPR. The headline number is the partial Spearman correlation controlling for the share of the language in CommonCrawl. The hypothesis is refuted by the condition fixed in advance: the sign disagrees between the two sources. The sign of the correlation is set by the language the detector was fine-tuned on, so fertility stands in for the distance between the training language and the language under test. Under a detector fine-tuned on Russian, English ranks last of 10 languages while having the lowest fertility of all 10.

title: Evaluating parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models for sentiment analysis with bayesian optimization
abstract: The increasing volume of user-generated reviews and feedback available in digital format provides valuable insights across various domains. Sentiment analysis plays a crucial role in extracting opinions from textual data. Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional performance in numerous Natural Language Processing tasks; however, fine-tuning these models remains resource-intensive and time-consuming. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques offer a more computationally efficient alternative. This study investigates the effectiveness of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for fine-tuning LLMs in Arabic sentiment analysis by evaluating both sequence classification and instruction-tuning paradigms across the ASTD, LABR, and HARD datasets. The results show that LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct achieves competitive performance compared to LLaMA-3-8B with a classification head. Moreover, SILMA-9B-Instruct shows the highest overall performance, achieving F1-scores of 88.95%, 89.91%, and 96.55% on ASTD, LABR, and HARD respectively. In addition, Bayesian hyperparameter optimization is employed to find optimal LoRA configurations by exploring rank, dropout, and learning rate so that maximum validation scores can be achieved with respect to the F1-score for the entire model.

title: Domain Adaptation via Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and Adversarial Domain Discriminators for Graph Neural Network Transfer Learning
abstract: Domain adaptation mitigates the severe problem of generalizing machine learning models that are trained on source domains to new target domains that exhibit substantial distributional shifts and significant differences in class-conditional distributions. This chapter reveals a joint scheme between the distance metric of maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) distance and adversarial domain discriminators to acquire unsupervised domain adaptation and maintain discriminative task-specific order. The MMD provides a positive-definite distance measure of distributional similarity in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, enabling quantification and minimization of distribution divergence without requiring explicit density estimation. Convergence analysis showed that learning curves were stable with the same amount of improvement in performance over the course of training. The convergence rate of the MMD-adversarial model was 50–100 epochs, which is significantly less than the average of 150–250 epochs of the base models.

title: A Unified Policy Architecture (UPA): The Governance Kernel for Enterprise AI Operating Systems
abstract: Enterprise AI is evolving into an Enterprise Operating System where autonomous AI agents can plan, reason, use memory, invoke tools, execute workflows, and collaborate with other agents. This shift creates a new governance challenge: existing authorization, security, guardrails, and compliance mechanisms are fragmented and are not designed to govern autonomous AI as a unified system. This paper introduces the Unified Policy Architecture (UPA), a governance architecture for Enterprise AI Operating Systems. UPA provides a unified policy model for governing AI and agents, tools, workflows, memory, enterprise resources, and agent-to-agent interactions and enterprise business rules. It extends policy control beyond authorisation to include runtime obligations, human approvals, compliance, audit evidence, and governance evaluation. We present UPA's governance model, declarative policy language foundations, policy evaluation semantics, extensible plugins, industry policy packs, and an evaluation framework for enterprise governance. We also identify extensions for multi-agent coordination, provenance-aware policies, and stateful runtime governance. UPA provides a foundation for building secure, accountable, and governable Enterprise Operating Systems for autonomous AI.

title: Supplementary Materials for "Generation Z's Response to AI-Generated Promotional Banner for MSMEs F&B: An Exploratory Qualitative Study"
abstract: This repository contains the supplementary research materials supporting the study "Generation Z's Response to AI-Generated Promotional Banner for MSMEs F&B: An Exploratory Qualitative Study." The study investigates how Generation Z consumers perceive, interpret, and respond to AI-generated promotional banners used by Food and Beverage (F&B) Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), examined through the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) framework across participants' cognitive, affective, and behavioural reactions. The dataset includes the interview guide used to conduct semi-structured interviews, anonymized transcripts of interviews with seven Generation Z participants (P1–P7), and a README file describing the contents, structure, and usage guidelines of the repository.

abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum self-organized networks (QSON) reinforcement learning, leveraging quantum entanglement and coherence to enhance learning strategies and improve the performance of reinforcement learning agents. We propose a framework that integrates quantum entanglement and self-consistency to optimize learning, thereby achieving superior results compared to existing methods. This work presents a significant advancement in reinforcement learning, demonstrating the potential for quantum-enhanced learning through the application of QSON principles.

abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithmic framework for the dynamic evolution of quantum states, specifically designed to optimize complex quantum systems, including those relevant to quantum information storage and transmission. This work addresses a long-standing challenge in quantum information science – the need for adaptive topological structures – offering a promising pathway towards more efficient and robust quantum systems.

TCA leverages the inherent topological structure of data clusters to proactively construct these clusters, ensuring high-quality and consistent clustering, and effectively handling high-dimensional data. The algorithm's core mechanism centers around learning a graph structure that guides the formation of clusters, avoiding the often-problematic "cold start" phenomenon inherent in many existing techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TCA through extensive experimental testing, showcasing its superior performance in various datasets and highlighting its ability to maintain cluster consistency and quality.
